text: The four-layer architecture of the HISE framework
body:
HISE is built around a **hierarchical processor tree**. Every project — sampler, synth, or effect — is a tree of processors that generate, modify, and route audio and MIDI. This page lays out the full architecture: the four layers that make up the framework, the processor types that populate the tree, and how everything fits together.

## The Four Layers

<!-- GRAPHIC: Architectural diagram — four layers as horizontal bands. Module Tree at the base (widest), Scripting and UI above it, Scriptnode as an overlay on the Module Tree, Sampling Engine as a specialization within. Arrows showing interactions between layers. -->

| Layer | What It Does | Where You Work |
|-------|-------------|----------------|
| **Module Tree** | Defines the audio architecture as a processor hierarchy | Module Tree Editor in the IDE |
| **Scripting** | Adds logic — UI, MIDI processing, parameter connections, state | Code Editor (HiseScript) |
| **Scriptnode** | Custom DSP processing via node graphs | Scriptnode Editor |
| **Sampling Engine** | Disk-streaming sample playback with mapping, compression, multi-mic | Sample Map Editor |

These layers are complementary. A sampler project uses all four: the module tree defines how samplers, effects, and modulators connect; scripts build the UI and handle articulation logic; scriptnode adds custom DSP when the built-in effects aren't enough; and the sampling engine manages disk streaming and sample mapping. A synth project might skip sampling entirely. An effect plugin might skip scriptnode.

The layer you reach for depends on what you need:

- **Module tree alone** produces sound — you can build a working synth by dragging processors into the tree and never writing a line of code.
- **Scripting** becomes necessary the moment you need a UI, MIDI logic, or parameter connections beyond what the IDE's visual tools handle.
- **Scriptnode** enters when you need DSP that doesn't exist as a built-in module — a custom filter topology, a Faust reverb algorithm, or a compiled C++ effect.
- **The sampling engine** enters when your project plays back recorded audio — sample libraries, drum kits, impulse responses.

## The Processor Taxonomy

Every node in the module tree is a **processor**. Four types exist, and they follow strict nesting rules:

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── MidiProcessorChain                          ← MIDI Processors live here
│   └── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
├── ModulatorSampler "Sustain"                  ← Sound Generator
│   ├── GainModulation                          ← Modulators attach to chains
│   │   ├── AhdsrEnvelope "VolumeEnv"
│   │   └── Velocity "VelMod"
│   ├── PitchModulation
│   │   └── LFO "Vibrato"
│   └── EffectChain                             ← Effects live inside generators...
│       └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"
└── EffectChain                                 ← ...or on the master chain
    ├── SimpleReverb "Reverb"
    └── Limiter "Output"
```

| Type | Role | Lives Inside | Examples |
|------|------|-------------|---------|
| **Sound Generators** | Produce audio | `SynthChain`, `SynthGroup` | `StreamingSampler`, `WaveSynth`, `WavetableSynth`, `SineSynth`, `AudioLooper` |
| **Modulators** | Shape parameters over time | `GainModulation`, `PitchModulation`, `FXModulation` chains | `AhdsrEnvelope`, `LFO`, `Velocity`, `MidiController`, `Random` |
| **Effects** | Process audio | `EffectChain` (inside a generator or on the master) | `PolyphonicFilter`, `SimpleReverb`, `Convolution`, `Delay`, `SimpleGain`, `CurveEq` |
| **MIDI Processors** | Transform MIDI before it reaches generators | `MidiProcessorChain` | `ScriptProcessor`, `Transposer`, `MidiMuter` |

Every sound generator has three internal chains: **GainModulation** (amplitude), **PitchModulation** (tuning), and **EffectChain** (per-voice processing). Modulators attach to the first two. Effects go in the third. This structure is fixed — you fill it, but you don't change it.

## Per-Voice vs Master

This is the single most important architectural concept in HISE. Where you place a processor determines whether it runs **per-voice** (polyphonic, inside a sound generator) or on the **master chain** (once, on the summed output).

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── StreamingSampler "Sustain"
│   └── EffectChain
│       └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"     ← runs per-voice: each note gets its own filter
└── EffectChain
    └── SimpleReverb "Reverb"              ← runs once on the summed stereo output
```

The distinction drives both **sound design** and **CPU usage**:

| Per-Voice (inside generator) | Master (on `SynthChain`) |
|------------------------------|------------------------|
| `PolyphonicFilter` — independent cutoff per note | `SimpleReverb`, `Convolution` — shared space |
| `AhdsrEnvelope` — amplitude contour per note | `CurveEq`, `Dynamics` — master tone shaping |
| `PolyshapeFX` — per-note saturation | `Limiter` — output protection |
| `SimpleGain` — per-mic level control | Mid/Side encoding (`LR2MS` / `MS2LR`) |

Per-voice effects multiply with polyphony — 16 voices with a per-voice filter means 16 filter instances. Master effects always run exactly once. Place effects at the right level from the start; moving them later changes your sound.

## The Three DSP Tiers

When you need audio processing, HISE offers three tiers of increasing flexibility:

| Tier | What | When To Use |
|------|------|-------------|
| **Tier 1 — Built-in modules** | Drag-and-drop processors from the module list | Standard effects (reverb, delay, EQ, filters, compression). Covers most needs. |
| **Tier 2 — Scriptnode stock nodes** | Build DSP graphs in the visual scriptnode editor | Custom signal routing, multi-band processing, parameter mapping, Faust integration. |
| **Tier 3 — Custom C++/Faust** | Write your own DSP as C++ header files or Faust code | Novel algorithms, performance-critical paths, proprietary DSP. Compiles to native code. |

Most projects live entirely in Tier 1. Of 13 analyzed shipping plugins, 4 use no scriptnode at all. The ones that do use it for things built-in modules can't do: true stereo convolution routing, custom resonance modeling, granular processing. Start with Tier 1; escalate when you hit its limits.

<!-- GRAPHIC: Visual showing the 3 tiers as concentric layers — Tier 1 (built-in) as the largest/simplest, Tier 2 (scriptnode) wrapping around it, Tier 3 (C++/Faust) as the outermost. Arrow labels: "drag-and-drop", "visual patching", "write code". -->

## Standard Architectures

While every project is different, three patterns recur across real-world HISE products. These are starting points, not constraints — you adapt them to your project.

**Sampler** — parallel `StreamingSampler` processors per articulation, modulators for envelopes and dynamics, MIDI processors for keyswitch logic:

```
SynthChain → MidiProcessorChain → [Interface + Articulation Handler]
           → StreamingSampler "Sustain" → [AHDSR + Velocity] + [Filter]
           → StreamingSampler "Staccato" → [AHDSR + Velocity]
           → EffectChain → [Reverb]
```

**Synth** — oscillators grouped in a `SynthGroup`, per-voice effects and modulation, master FX chain:

```
SynthChain → ScriptProcessor "Interface"
           → SynthGroup → WavetableSynth "OSC1" → [AHDSR + Velocity + LFO] + [Filter]
           → EffectChain → [Delay + Reverb]
```

**Effect** — no generators, just an effect chain processing incoming DAW audio:

```
SynthChain → ScriptProcessor "Interface"
           → EffectChain → [Convolution + CurveEQ + SimpleGain]
```

These architectures are covered in full detail — with nesting rules, container types, and real-world variations — in [The Module Tree](/v2/architecture/module-tree).

## How the Layers Connect

In practice, here's how the layers interact during development. Consider a sampler plugin:

1. **Module tree**: you add a `StreamingSampler`, an `AhdsrEnvelope` on its gain chain, a `PolyphonicFilter` in its effect chain, and a `SimpleReverb` on the master chain.
2. **Sampling engine**: you import audio files into the Sample Map Editor, map them across the keyboard with velocity layers, and save the SampleMap.
3. **Scripting**: you write `Content.makeFrontInterface()` in a `ScriptProcessor`, add knobs for filter cutoff and reverb mix, and connect them to the module parameters.
4. **Scriptnode** *(optional)*: you build a custom resonance network in the scriptnode editor and host it as a `HardcodedMasterFX`.

Each layer touches different files on disk: the module tree lives in your project's main `.xml` preset, scripts live in `Scripts/`, sample maps in `SampleMaps/`, and DSP networks in `DspNetworks/`. They converge at runtime into a single audio processing graph.

<!-- CODE_EXAMPLE: A minimal 8-line interface script that references a module and connects a knob — showing the scripting ↔ module tree connection in action -->

## What's Next

- **Next →** [The Module Tree](/v2/architecture/module-tree) — nesting rules, containers, and the standard architectures in full detail
- **Next →** [Signal Flow](/v2/architecture/audio-signal-path) — how audio and MIDI move through the tree, modulation basics, and per-voice vs master
- **Next →** [The Scripting Model](/v2/architecture/scripting-model) — how scripts wire the module tree, UI, and presets together
- **Build one →** [Building a Sampler](/v2/guide/building-a-sampler), [Building a Synth](/v2/guide/building-a-synth), or [Building an Effect](/v2/guide/building-an-effect)

|------|------|-------------|---------|
| **Sound Generators** | Produce audio | `SynthChain`, `SynthGroup` | `StreamingSampler`, `WaveSynth`, `WavetableSynth`, `SineSynth`, `AudioLooper` |
| **Modulators** | Shape parameters over time | `GainModulation`, `PitchModulation`, `FXModulation` chains | `AhdsrEnvelope`, `LFO`, `Velocity`, `MidiController`, `Random` |
| **Effects** | Process audio | `EffectChain` (inside a generator or on the master) | `PolyphonicFilter`, `SimpleReverb`, `Convolution`, `Delay`, `SimpleGain`, `CurveEq` |
| **MIDI Processors** | Transform MIDI before it reaches generators | `MidiProcessorChain` | `ScriptProcessor`, `Transposer`, `MidiMuter` |

Every sound generator has three internal chains: **GainModulation** (amplitude), **PitchModulation** (tuning), and **EffectChain** (per-voice processing). Modulators attach to the first two. Effects go in the third. This structure is fixed — you fill it, but you don't change it.

text:
Per-Voice vs Master

This is the single most important architectural concept in HISE. Where you place a processor determines whether it runs **per-voice** (polyphonic, inside a sound generator) or on the **master chain** (once, on the summed output).

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── StreamingSampler "Sustain"
│   └── EffectChain
│       └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"     ← runs per-voice: each note gets its own filter
└── EffectChain
    └── SimpleReverb "Reverb"              ← runs once on the summed stereo output
```

The distinction drives both **sound design** and **CPU usage**:

| Per-Voice (inside generator) | Master (on `SynthChain`) |
|------------------------------|------------------------|
| `PolyphonicFilter` — independent cutoff per note | `SimpleReverb`, `Convolution` — shared space |
| `AhdsrEnvelope` — amplitude contour per note | `CurveEq`, `Dynamics` — master tone shaping |
| `PolyshapeFX` — per-note saturation | `Limiter` — output protection |
| `SimpleGain` — per-mic level control | Mid/Side encoding (`LR2MS` / `MS2LR`) |

Per-voice effects multiply with polyphony — 16 voices with a per-voice filter means 16 filter instances. Master effects always run exactly once. Place effects at the right level from the start; moving them later changes your sound.

text:
The Three DSP Tiers

When you need audio processing, HISE offers three tiers of increasing flexibility:

| Tier | What | When To Use |
|------|------|-------------|
| **Tier 1 — Built-in modules** | Drag-and-drop processors from the module list | Standard effects (reverb, delay, EQ, filters, compression). Covers most needs. |
| **Tier 2 — Scriptnode stock nodes** | Build DSP graphs in the visual scriptnode editor | Custom signal routing, multi-band processing, parameter mapping, Faust integration. |
| **Tier 3 — Custom C++/Faust** | Write your own DSP as C++ header files or Faust code | Novel algorithms, performance-critical paths, proprietary DSP. Compiles to native code. |

Most projects live entirely in Tier 1. Of 13 analyzed shipping plugins, 4 use no scriptnode at all. The ones that do use it for things built-in modules can't do: true stereo convolution routing, custom resonance modeling, granular processing. Start with Tier 1; escalate when you hit its limits.

text:
Standard Architectures

While every project is different, three patterns recur across real-world HISE products. These are starting points, not constraints — you adapt them to your project.

**Sampler** — parallel `StreamingSampler` processors per articulation, modulators for envelopes and dynamics, MIDI processors for keyswitch logic:

```
SynthChain → MidiProcessorChain → [Interface + Articulation Handler]
           → StreamingSampler "Sustain" → [AHDSR + Velocity] + [Filter]
           → StreamingSampler "Staccato" → [AHDSR + Velocity]
           → EffectChain → [Reverb]
```

**Synth** — oscillators grouped in a `SynthGroup`, per-voice effects and modulation, master FX chain:

```
SynthChain → ScriptProcessor "Interface"
           → SynthGroup → WavetableSynth "OSC1" → [AHDSR + Velocity + LFO] + [Filter]
           → EffectChain → [Delay + Reverb]
```

**Effect** — no generators, just an effect chain processing incoming DAW audio:

```
SynthChain → ScriptProcessor "Interface"
           → EffectChain → [Convolution + CurveEQ + SimpleGain]
```

These architectures are covered in full detail — with nesting rules, container types, and real-world variations — in [The Module Tree](/v2/architecture/module-tree).

text:
How the Layers Connect

In practice, here's how the layers interact during development. Consider a sampler plugin:

1. **Module tree**: you add a `StreamingSampler`, an `AhdsrEnvelope` on its gain chain, a `PolyphonicFilter` in its effect chain, and a `SimpleReverb` on the master chain.
2. **Sampling engine**: you import audio files into the Sample Map Editor, map them across the keyboard with velocity layers, and save the SampleMap.
3. **Scripting**: you write `Content.makeFrontInterface()` in a `ScriptProcessor`, add knobs for filter cutoff and reverb mix, and connect them to the module parameters.
4. **Scriptnode** *(optional)*: you build a custom resonance network in the scriptnode editor and host it as a `HardcodedMasterFX`.

Each layer touches different files on disk: the module tree lives in your project's main `.xml` preset, scripts live in `Scripts/`, sample maps in `SampleMaps/`, and DSP networks in `DspNetworks/`. They converge at runtime into a single audio processing graph.

<!-- CODE_EXAMPLE: A minimal 8-line interface script that references a module and connects a knob — showing the scripting ↔ module tree connection in action -->

text: Processor types, internal chains, containers, nesting rules, and standard architectures
body:
Every HISE instrument is a **module tree** — a hierarchy of processors that defines your complete audio architecture. This tree determines how MIDI flows in, where sound generates, how modulation shapes it, and where effects process the output. You don't write imperative audio routing code. You build a tree, and the engine interprets it as a live signal graph.

Understanding this tree is understanding HISE. Every decision you make — where to place a filter, how to route modulation, whether an effect runs per-voice or on the master — comes down to where something sits in this tree.

The tree lives in two places: the **Module Tree Editor** in the IDE (visual drag-and-drop) and the **XML preset file** on disk. They are the same data. The IDE edits the tree visually; the XML serializes it.


## The Four Processor Types

Every node in the module tree is one of four types:

![The four processor types in signal order](/images/v2/architecture/processor-types-overview.svg)

| Type | Role | Where it lives | Examples |
|------|------|----------------|----------|
| **Sound Generators** | Produce audio | `SynthChain`, `SynthGroup` | `StreamingSampler`, `WavetableSynth`, `WaveSynth`, `SineSynth`, `AudioLooper` |
| **Modulators** | Shape parameters over time | `GainModulation`, `PitchModulation`, `FXModulation` chains | `AhdsrEnvelope`, `LFO`, `Velocity`, `MidiController`, `Random`, `KeyNumber` |
| **Effects** | Process existing audio | `EffectChain` (per-voice or master) | `PolyphonicFilter`, `SimpleReverb`, `Convolution`, `Delay`, `CurveEq`, `Limiter` |
| **MIDI Processors** | Transform MIDI before it reaches generators | `MidiProcessorChain` | `ScriptProcessor`, `Transposer`, `MidiMuter` |

These types follow **strict nesting rules.** You can't place a `SimpleReverb` inside a `GainModulation` chain, or an `AhdsrEnvelope` inside an `EffectChain`. The IDE enforces this — grayed-out drop targets mean the processor doesn't belong there.

The constraints aren't arbitrary. The tree IS the signal flow. A processor's position tells the engine exactly what to do with it: something inside `GainModulation` is a modulation source for amplitude; the same thing inside `EffectChain` would be meaningless. The nesting rules make every tree unambiguous.


## Every Generator's Blueprint: The Four Internal Chains

This is the most important structural concept in HISE.

Every sound generator — `StreamingSampler`, `WavetableSynth`, `SineSynth`, anything — has the same internal skeleton: **four fixed chains**, always in the same order.

![The four internal chains of every sound generator](/images/v2/architecture/generator-blueprint.svg)

```
StreamingSampler "Piano"
├── MidiProcessorChain                    ← ① Transforms MIDI before voice allocation
│   ├── ScriptProcessor "VelocityCurve"
│   └── Transposer "OctaveShift"
├── GainModulation                        ← ② Shapes amplitude (envelopes, velocity)
│   ├── AhdsrEnvelope "VolumeEnv"
│   └── Velocity "VelMod"
├── PitchModulation                       ← ③ Shapes tuning (vibrato, pitch bend)
│   ├── LFO "Vibrato"
│   └── PitchWheel "Bend"
├── EffectChain                           ← ④ Processes per-voice audio (filter, gain)
│   ├── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"
│   └── SimpleGain "Level"
```

The order corresponds to the processing sequence:

1. **MidiProcessorChain** runs first — it can block notes, remap velocity, or shift pitch before the engine allocates a voice.
2. The voice starts, and **GainModulation** shapes the voice's amplitude continuously.
3. **PitchModulation** shapes the voice's tuning — vibrato, pitch bend, key tracking.
4. **EffectChain** processes the voice's audio output — per-voice filters, saturation, gain staging.

Why is this structure fixed? Because it eliminates ambiguity. The position alone tells the engine everything. Every generator works identically, which means patterns you learn on one transfer directly to all others.

::Tip{title="Tree order = data structure order"}
The four internal chains always appear **before** any child audio modules in both the XML and the Module Tree Editor. Diagrams in this documentation always match the XML order.
::

**Empty chains still exist.** If you don't add anything to a generator's `PitchModulation` chain, it's still present — it just does nothing and costs no CPU. You can add a vibrato LFO to any generator at any time by dropping it into the already-existing chain. No restructuring needed.


## Container Types

Three container types determine how processors combine.

![The three container types compared](/images/v2/architecture/container-types.svg)

### SynthChain — Parallel Sound Sources

`SynthChain` is the root of every HISE project and can also appear nested. Its child generators render **in parallel** — each produces audio independently, and the outputs sum together.

Use it for **independent sound sources that blend.** A multi-articulation sampler has a `StreamingSampler` per articulation (sustain, staccato, legato), all inside the root SynthChain. A complex instrument might nest SynthChains to group sections with their own effects and modulation.

`SynthChain` is the only container with a **master EffectChain**. Effects placed in the root SynthChain's EffectChain process the summed output of all generators — reverbs, master EQ, compression, and limiters live here.

### SynthGroup — Voice-Grouped Synthesis

`SynthGroup` solves a specific problem: multiple oscillators that should behave as **one voice**.

In a `SynthChain`, each child generator manages voice allocation independently — a note-on creates a separate voice in each generator. In a `SynthGroup`, all children **share the same voice**. This is essential for synthesizers where oscillators should detune, cross-modulate, or share envelopes.

`SynthGroup` also has two extra modulation chains that no other container provides:

- **DetuneModulation** — pitch spread between voices (unison detune)
- **SpreadModulation** — stereo width between voices

A 3-oscillator wavetable synth groups its oscillators in a `SynthGroup` so they share voice allocation. A Hammond simulation places 36 `SineSynth` oscillators inside one so they all play as a single voice. Even a single-oscillator design benefits if it needs unison detune and spread.

### EffectChain — Serial Audio Processing

`EffectChain` processes effects in **strict series**: the output of Effect 1 becomes the input of Effect 2. Order matters — EQ before compression sounds different from compression before EQ.

EffectChains appear in two positions with fundamentally different behavior:

| Position | Runs | CPU cost | Behavior |
|----------|------|----------|----------|
| **Inside a generator** (per-voice) | Once per active voice | Multiplies with polyphony | Each note has independent processing |
| **On a SynthChain** (master) | Once on the summed output | Fixed | All notes share the same processing |

A `PolyphonicFilter` inside a generator gives **each note its own filter** — 16 voices means 16 independent filter instances. The same filter on the master chain processes all 16 notes as one signal. This per-voice vs master distinction drives both your sound design and your CPU budget.

The rule of thumb: **per-voice for things that differ per note** (filters, envelopes, saturation), **master for things that are shared** (reverb, delay, limiting, EQ).


## Standard Architectures

Three patterns cover the vast majority of HISE projects. They're starting templates — adapt them to what your instrument needs.

### Sampler Architecture

For sample libraries, orchestral instruments, pianos — anything built around recorded audio:

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── MidiProcessorChain
│   ├── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
│   ├── ScriptProcessor "ArticulationHandler"
│   └── ScriptProcessor "CC64Handler"
├── GainModulation
│   ├── Velocity "VelocityMod"
│   └── MidiController "ExpressionCC"
├── PitchModulation
├── EffectChain
│   ├── SimpleReverb "Ambience"
│   └── SimpleGain "MasterLevel"
│
├── StreamingSampler "Sustain"                     ← primary articulation
│   ├── MidiProcessorChain
│   ├── GainModulation
│   │   └── AhdsrEnvelope "SustainEnv"
│   ├── PitchModulation
│   └── EffectChain
│       └── SimpleGain "SustainLevel"
│
└── StreamingSampler "Staccato"                    ← alternate articulation
    ├── MidiProcessorChain
    ├── GainModulation
    │   └── AhdsrEnvelope "StaccatoEnv"
    ├── PitchModulation
    └── EffectChain
        └── SimpleGain "StaccatoLevel"
```

The pattern: one `StreamingSampler` per articulation, all as children of the root SynthChain. MIDI muter logic switches which sampler receives MIDI via keyswitches. Root-level GainModulation handles global dynamics. Each sampler has its own envelope and level. The master EffectChain runs reverb and output gain on the combined result.

Multi-mic instruments extend this with parallel `SimpleGain` effects per sampler — one per mic position (close, room, far), each independently level-controlled and purgeable.

### Synthesizer Architecture

For wavetable, subtractive, FM, or hybrid synths:

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── MidiProcessorChain
│   └── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
├── GainModulation
├── PitchModulation
├── EffectChain
│   ├── Delay "StereoDelay"
│   ├── SimpleReverb "Hall"
│   └── Limiter "Output"
│
└── SynthGroup "Oscillators"                       ← voice-grouped
    ├── MidiProcessorChain
    ├── GainModulation
    ├── PitchModulation
    ├── EffectChain
    ├── DetuneModulation
    │   └── LFO "UnisonDetune"
    │
    ├── WavetableSynth "OSC1"
    │   ├── MidiProcessorChain
    │   ├── GainModulation
    │   │   └── AhdsrEnvelope "Amp1"
    │   ├── PitchModulation
    │   │   └── LFO "Vibrato1"
    │   └── EffectChain
    │       └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter1"         ← per-voice filter
    │
    └── WavetableSynth "OSC2"
        ├── MidiProcessorChain
        ├── GainModulation
        │   └── AhdsrEnvelope "Amp2"
        ├── PitchModulation
        │   └── LFO "Vibrato2"
        └── EffectChain
            └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter2"         ← per-voice filter
```

`SynthGroup` wraps the oscillators so one MIDI note activates both simultaneously. Each oscillator has independent envelopes and per-voice filtering. `DetuneModulation` adds unison spread. Time-based effects and the limiter live on the master EffectChain.

### Effect Plugin Architecture

For reverbs, delays, EQ suites — anything that processes incoming audio without generating its own:

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── MidiProcessorChain
│   └── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
├── GainModulation
├── PitchModulation
└── EffectChain
    ├── CurveEq "PreEQ"
    ├── Convolution "MainReverb"
    ├── Delay "PreDelay"
    ├── CurveEq "PostEQ"
    └── SimpleGain "OutputLevel"
```

No sound generators. The root SynthChain receives audio from the DAW host and passes it through a serial EffectChain. Effect order is deliberate: input shaping → core processing → enhancement → output shaping → level.


## Container Patterns

Six patterns recur across real-world HISE instruments:

| Pattern | What it does | When to use it |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| **MIDI Muter switching** | `MidiMuter` toggles which generators receive MIDI | Articulation switching via keyswitches |
| **Nested SynthChains** | `SynthChain` inside `SynthChain` | Grouping sections with independent routing and effects |
| **GlobalModulatorContainer** | Shared modulation sources accessible across the tree | One LFO modulating multiple oscillators |
| **SlotFX** | A swappable effect slot inside an EffectChain | User-selectable effects at runtime |
| **SendContainer + SendFX** | Auxiliary send/return routing | Shared reverb sends with per-generator send levels |
| **Parallel voices** | Multiple generators as siblings in one SynthChain | Layered instruments (sustain + release triggers + noise) |

**MIDI Muter switching** deserves special attention for sample libraries. The naive approach to articulation switching — loading a different sample map on keyswitch — causes audible gaps because of disk I/O. The muter pattern keeps every articulation loaded simultaneously as parallel `StreamingSampler` processors, then uses `MidiMuter` to silence all but the active one. The switch is instantaneous because no samples need to load.

**GlobalModulatorContainer** enables the [Modulation System](/v2/architecture/modulation-system)'s most powerful feature: shared modulation sources. Without it, a LFO inside one generator only affects that generator. With a `GlobalModulatorContainer` at the root level, any generator in the tree can reference shared modulation sources — enabling user-configurable routing through the modulation matrix.


## The XML Behind the Tree

The Module Tree Editor and the XML file are the same data. A brief look at the correspondence helps when reading project files:

```xml
<Processor Type="SynthChain" ID="Master Chain">
  <ChildProcessors>
    <Processor Type="MidiProcessorChain" ID="Midi Processor">
      <ChildProcessors>
        <Processor Type="ScriptProcessor" ID="Interface"/>
      </ChildProcessors>
    </Processor>
    <Processor Type="ModulatorChain" ID="GainModulation"/>
    <Processor Type="ModulatorChain" ID="PitchModulation"/>
    <Processor Type="EffectChain" ID="FX"/>
    <Processor Type="StreamingSampler" ID="Sampler"/>
  </ChildProcessors>
</Processor>
```

Each `<Processor>` tag maps to a node. The `Type` selects the processor; the `ID` is the name you use from scripts (e.g., `Synth.getEffect("FX")`). The order in XML matches the order in the IDE — four internal chains first, then child audio modules.


## What's Next

The module tree defines **what** processors exist and **where** they connect. Next, understand **how** audio and MIDI move through this tree at runtime.

- **Next →** [Signal Flow](/v2/architecture/audio-signal-path) — voice allocation, the render pipeline, per-voice vs master, and basic modulation
- **Deep dive →** [The Modulation System](/v2/architecture/modulation-system) — global modulators, the modulation matrix, and advanced routing
- **Build one →** [Building a Sampler](/v2/guide/building-a-sampler) — apply the sampler architecture to a real project
- **Build one →** [Building a Synth](/v2/guide/building-a-synth) — apply the synthesizer architecture
- **Build one →** [Building an Effect](/v2/guide/building-an-effect) — apply the effect plugin architecture

|------|------|----------------|----------|
| **Sound Generators** | Produce audio | `SynthChain`, `SynthGroup` | `StreamingSampler`, `WavetableSynth`, `WaveSynth`, `SineSynth`, `AudioLooper` |
| **Modulators** | Shape parameters over time | `GainModulation`, `PitchModulation`, `FXModulation` chains | `AhdsrEnvelope`, `LFO`, `Velocity`, `MidiController`, `Random`, `KeyNumber` |
| **Effects** | Process existing audio | `EffectChain` (per-voice or master) | `PolyphonicFilter`, `SimpleReverb`, `Convolution`, `Delay`, `CurveEq`, `Limiter` |
| **MIDI Processors** | Transform MIDI before it reaches generators | `MidiProcessorChain` | `ScriptProcessor`, `Transposer`, `MidiMuter` |

These types follow **strict nesting rules.** You can't place a `SimpleReverb` inside a `GainModulation` chain, or an `AhdsrEnvelope` inside an `EffectChain`. The IDE enforces this — grayed-out drop targets mean the processor doesn't belong there.

text:
Every Generator's Blueprint: The Four Internal Chains

This is the most important structural concept in HISE.

Every sound generator — `StreamingSampler`, `WavetableSynth`, `SineSynth`, anything — has the same internal skeleton: **four fixed chains**, always in the same order.

![The four internal chains of every sound generator](/images/v2/architecture/generator-blueprint.svg)

```
StreamingSampler "Piano"
├── MidiProcessorChain                    ← ① Transforms MIDI before voice allocation
│   ├── ScriptProcessor "VelocityCurve"
│   └── Transposer "OctaveShift"
├── GainModulation                        ← ② Shapes amplitude (envelopes, velocity)
│   ├── AhdsrEnvelope "VolumeEnv"
│   └── Velocity "VelMod"
├── PitchModulation                       ← ③ Shapes tuning (vibrato, pitch bend)
│   ├── LFO "Vibrato"
│   └── PitchWheel "Bend"
├── EffectChain                           ← ④ Processes per-voice audio (filter, gain)
│   ├── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"
│   └── SimpleGain "Level"
```

The order corresponds to the processing sequence:

1. **MidiProcessorChain** runs first — it can block notes, remap velocity, or shift pitch before the engine allocates a voice.
2. The voice starts, and **GainModulation** shapes the voice's amplitude continuously.
3. **PitchModulation** shapes the voice's tuning — vibrato, pitch bend, key tracking.
4. **EffectChain** processes the voice's audio output — per-voice filters, saturation, gain staging.

Why is this structure fixed? Because it eliminates ambiguity. The position alone tells the engine everything. Every generator works identically, which means patterns you learn on one transfer directly to all others.



**Empty chains still exist.** If you don't add anything to a generator's `PitchModulation` chain, it's still present — it just does nothing and costs no CPU. You can add a vibrato LFO to any generator at any time by dropping it into the already-existing chain. No restructuring needed.

text:
Container Types

Three container types determine how processors combine.

![The three container types compared](/images/v2/architecture/container-types.svg)

### SynthChain — Parallel Sound Sources

`SynthChain` is the root of every HISE project and can also appear nested. Its child generators render **in parallel** — each produces audio independently, and the outputs sum together.

Use it for **independent sound sources that blend.** A multi-articulation sampler has a `StreamingSampler` per articulation (sustain, staccato, legato), all inside the root SynthChain. A complex instrument might nest SynthChains to group sections with their own effects and modulation.

`SynthChain` is the only container with a **master EffectChain**. Effects placed in the root SynthChain's EffectChain process the summed output of all generators — reverbs, master EQ, compression, and limiters live here.

### SynthGroup — Voice-Grouped Synthesis

`SynthGroup` solves a specific problem: multiple oscillators that should behave as **one voice**.

In a `SynthChain`, each child generator manages voice allocation independently — a note-on creates a separate voice in each generator. In a `SynthGroup`, all children **share the same voice**. This is essential for synthesizers where oscillators should detune, cross-modulate, or share envelopes.

`SynthGroup` also has two extra modulation chains that no other container provides:

- **DetuneModulation** — pitch spread between voices (unison detune)
- **SpreadModulation** — stereo width between voices

A 3-oscillator wavetable synth groups its oscillators in a `SynthGroup` so they share voice allocation. A Hammond simulation places 36 `SineSynth` oscillators inside one so they all play as a single voice. Even a single-oscillator design benefits if it needs unison detune and spread.

### EffectChain — Serial Audio Processing

`EffectChain` processes effects in **strict series**: the output of Effect 1 becomes the input of Effect 2. Order matters — EQ before compression sounds different from compression before EQ.

EffectChains appear in two positions with fundamentally different behavior:

| Position | Runs | CPU cost | Behavior |
|----------|------|----------|----------|
| **Inside a generator** (per-voice) | Once per active voice | Multiplies with polyphony | Each note has independent processing |
| **On a SynthChain** (master) | Once on the summed output | Fixed | All notes share the same processing |

A `PolyphonicFilter` inside a generator gives **each note its own filter** — 16 voices means 16 independent filter instances. The same filter on the master chain processes all 16 notes as one signal. This per-voice vs master distinction drives both your sound design and your CPU budget.

The rule of thumb: **per-voice for things that differ per note** (filters, envelopes, saturation), **master for things that are shared** (reverb, delay, limiting, EQ).

text:
Standard Architectures

Three patterns cover the vast majority of HISE projects. They're starting templates — adapt them to what your instrument needs.

### Sampler Architecture

For sample libraries, orchestral instruments, pianos — anything built around recorded audio:

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── MidiProcessorChain
│   ├── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
│   ├── ScriptProcessor "ArticulationHandler"
│   └── ScriptProcessor "CC64Handler"
├── GainModulation
│   ├── Velocity "VelocityMod"
│   └── MidiController "ExpressionCC"
├── PitchModulation
├── EffectChain
│   ├── SimpleReverb "Ambience"
│   └── SimpleGain "MasterLevel"
│
├── StreamingSampler "Sustain"                     ← primary articulation
│   ├── MidiProcessorChain
│   ├── GainModulation
│   │   └── AhdsrEnvelope "SustainEnv"
│   ├── PitchModulation
│   └── EffectChain
│       └── SimpleGain "SustainLevel"
│
└── StreamingSampler "Staccato"                    ← alternate articulation
    ├── MidiProcessorChain
    ├── GainModulation
    │   └── AhdsrEnvelope "StaccatoEnv"
    ├── PitchModulation
    └── EffectChain
        └── SimpleGain "StaccatoLevel"
```

The pattern: one `StreamingSampler` per articulation, all as children of the root SynthChain. MIDI muter logic switches which sampler receives MIDI via keyswitches. Root-level GainModulation handles global dynamics. Each sampler has its own envelope and level. The master EffectChain runs reverb and output gain on the combined result.

Multi-mic instruments extend this with parallel `SimpleGain` effects per sampler — one per mic position (close, room, far), each independently level-controlled and purgeable.

### Synthesizer Architecture

For wavetable, subtractive, FM, or hybrid synths:

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── MidiProcessorChain
│   └── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
├── GainModulation
├── PitchModulation
├── EffectChain
│   ├── Delay "StereoDelay"
│   ├── SimpleReverb "Hall"
│   └── Limiter "Output"
│
└── SynthGroup "Oscillators"                       ← voice-grouped
    ├── MidiProcessorChain
    ├── GainModulation
    ├── PitchModulation
    ├── EffectChain
    ├── DetuneModulation
    │   └── LFO "UnisonDetune"
    │
    ├── WavetableSynth "OSC1"
    │   ├── MidiProcessorChain
    │   ├── GainModulation
    │   │   └── AhdsrEnvelope "Amp1"
    │   ├── PitchModulation
    │   │   └── LFO "Vibrato1"
    │   └── EffectChain
    │       └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter1"         ← per-voice filter
    │
    └── WavetableSynth "OSC2"
        ├── MidiProcessorChain
        ├── GainModulation
        │   └── AhdsrEnvelope "Amp2"
        ├── PitchModulation
        │   └── LFO "Vibrato2"
        └── EffectChain
            └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter2"         ← per-voice filter
```

`SynthGroup` wraps the oscillators so one MIDI note activates both simultaneously. Each oscillator has independent envelopes and per-voice filtering. `DetuneModulation` adds unison spread. Time-based effects and the limiter live on the master EffectChain.

### Effect Plugin Architecture

For reverbs, delays, EQ suites — anything that processes incoming audio without generating its own:

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── MidiProcessorChain
│   └── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
├── GainModulation
├── PitchModulation
└── EffectChain
    ├── CurveEq "PreEQ"
    ├── Convolution "MainReverb"
    ├── Delay "PreDelay"
    ├── CurveEq "PostEQ"
    └── SimpleGain "OutputLevel"
```

No sound generators. The root SynthChain receives audio from the DAW host and passes it through a serial EffectChain. Effect order is deliberate: input shaping → core processing → enhancement → output shaping → level.

text:
Container Patterns

Six patterns recur across real-world HISE instruments:

| Pattern | What it does | When to use it |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| **MIDI Muter switching** | `MidiMuter` toggles which generators receive MIDI | Articulation switching via keyswitches |
| **Nested SynthChains** | `SynthChain` inside `SynthChain` | Grouping sections with independent routing and effects |
| **GlobalModulatorContainer** | Shared modulation sources accessible across the tree | One LFO modulating multiple oscillators |
| **SlotFX** | A swappable effect slot inside an EffectChain | User-selectable effects at runtime |
| **SendContainer + SendFX** | Auxiliary send/return routing | Shared reverb sends with per-generator send levels |
| **Parallel voices** | Multiple generators as siblings in one SynthChain | Layered instruments (sustain + release triggers + noise) |

**MIDI Muter switching** deserves special attention for sample libraries. The naive approach to articulation switching — loading a different sample map on keyswitch — causes audible gaps because of disk I/O. The muter pattern keeps every articulation loaded simultaneously as parallel `StreamingSampler` processors, then uses `MidiMuter` to silence all but the active one. The switch is instantaneous because no samples need to load.

**GlobalModulatorContainer** enables the [Modulation System](/v2/architecture/modulation-system)'s most powerful feature: shared modulation sources. Without it, a LFO inside one generator only affects that generator. With a `GlobalModulatorContainer` at the root level, any generator in the tree can reference shared modulation sources — enabling user-configurable routing through the modulation matrix.

text:
The XML Behind the Tree

The Module Tree Editor and the XML file are the same data. A brief look at the correspondence helps when reading project files:

```xml
<Processor Type="SynthChain" ID="Master Chain">
  <ChildProcessors>
    <Processor Type="MidiProcessorChain" ID="Midi Processor">
      <ChildProcessors>
        <Processor Type="ScriptProcessor" ID="Interface"/>
      </ChildProcessors>
    </Processor>
    <Processor Type="ModulatorChain" ID="GainModulation"/>
    <Processor Type="ModulatorChain" ID="PitchModulation"/>
    <Processor Type="EffectChain" ID="FX"/>
    <Processor Type="StreamingSampler" ID="Sampler"/>
  </ChildProcessors>
</Processor>
```

Each `<Processor>` tag maps to a node. The `Type` selects the processor; the `ID` is the name you use from scripts (e.g., `Synth.getEffect("FX")`). The order in XML matches the order in the IDE — four internal chains first, then child audio modules.

text: How audio and MIDI move through the module tree — from MIDI input to final output
body:
The module tree defines *what* processors exist and *where* they connect. Signal flow defines *how* audio and MIDI actually move through that tree at runtime — the sequence of operations that turns MIDI messages into audible sound, every audio buffer.

Understanding signal flow explains the "why" behind the module tree's structure. Why do the four internal chains appear in that order? Why does a filter inside a generator sound different from the same filter on the master chain? Why does voice count affect CPU? The answers are all here, in the render pipeline.


## MIDI Signal Flow

MIDI messages follow a predictable path through the tree before any audio renders:

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── MidiProcessorChain                            ← ① ALL incoming MIDI processed here first
│   ├── ScriptProcessor "Interface"               ← Keyswitch logic, global transforms
│   └── ScriptProcessor "Arpeggiator"             ← Can generate new MIDI events
├── GainModulation
├── PitchModulation
├── EffectChain
├── StreamingSampler "Sustain"
│   ├── MidiProcessorChain                        ← ② Generator-specific MIDI processing
│   │   └── Transposer "OctaveShift"
│   ├── GainModulation
│   ├── PitchModulation
│   └── EffectChain
└── StreamingSampler "Staccato"
    ├── MidiProcessorChain                        ← ② Each generator gets its own MIDI chain
    ├── GainModulation
    ├── PitchModulation
    └── EffectChain
```

The **root MidiProcessorChain** processes all incoming MIDI first. This is where your interface script sits — keyswitch logic, arpeggiators, velocity remapping, MIDI filtering. Any `ScriptProcessor` or `Transposer` here transforms MIDI before generators see it.

After root processing, MIDI flows to **each generator's internal MidiProcessorChain**. Generator-specific MIDI logic lives here — a velocity curve that only applies to one sampler, transposition for one oscillator, per-generator script logic.

Finally, processed MIDI triggers **voice allocation**. A `noteOn` message becomes a voice — a runtime object that will render audio for the duration of that note. A `noteOff` message signals the voice to enter its release phase.

The ordering matters. Root MIDI processing can block notes before they reach any generator — a `MidiMuter` at the root level prevents voice allocation entirely, which is how articulation switching works without wasting CPU on silent voices.


## The Audio Render Pipeline

Every audio buffer HISE processes follows four stages in sequence. This is the engine's heartbeat — it runs hundreds of times per second, once per audio buffer.

![Complete signal flow from MIDI input to audio output](/images/v2/architecture/signal-flow-overview.svg)

### Stage 1 — MIDI Processing

All MIDI messages for the current buffer are processed through the root `MidiProcessorChain`. The engine doesn't process the whole buffer as one block — it **splits the buffer at MIDI event timestamps** for sample-accurate timing. If a `noteOn` arrives at sample 247 of a 512-sample buffer, HISE renders samples 0–246, allocates the voice exactly at sample 247, then renders samples 247–511 with the new voice active.

This event-split approach means MIDI timing is precise to the individual sample, not quantized to the buffer boundary. For percussive instruments and tight rhythmic playing, this precision keeps transients locked to the grid.

### Stage 2 — Per-Voice Rendering

For each sub-block, every active voice renders in sequence:

1. **Gain modulation** calculates — `AhdsrEnvelope`, `Velocity`, `LFO` and any other modulators on the GainModulation chain produce amplitude values for this block
2. **Pitch modulation** calculates — vibrato `LFO`, `PitchWheel`, key tracking and any other modulators on the PitchModulation chain produce pitch offset values
3. **The generator renders audio** — the sampler or oscillator produces raw audio, shaped by the modulation values
4. **Per-voice effects process** — the generator's EffectChain processes this voice's audio independently

Voices **accumulate** — each voice adds its output to a shared buffer. When the last voice finishes rendering, the buffer contains the summed audio from all active voices.

This is why the four internal chains appear in the order they do. MIDI processing runs first (it determines what voices exist). Gain and pitch modulation calculate before the generator renders (the generator needs those values to shape its output). Per-voice effects run last (they process the audio the generator just produced). The tree structure mirrors the render sequence.

### Stage 3 — Summing

All per-voice audio accumulates into a single stereo buffer. This is where individual voices become a combined signal.

### Stage 4 — Master Effects

The master `EffectChain` on the SynthChain runs once on the combined output. This is where reverbs, master EQ, compression, and limiters process the final stereo signal. Master effects hear all voices together — they process after summing, not before.


## Per-Voice vs Master Processing

This is signal flow's most consequential concept. Where a processor sits in the tree determines *when* it runs, *how often* it runs, and *what audio* it hears.

![Per-voice processing vs master processing](/images/v2/architecture/signal-flow-per-voice-vs-master.svg)

| | Per-Voice (inside generator) | Master (on SynthChain) |
|---|---|---|
| **Runs** | Once per active voice, per buffer | Once on the summed output, per buffer |
| **CPU cost** | Multiplies with polyphony | Fixed, regardless of voice count |
| **Audio behavior** | Each note has independent processing state | All notes share the same processing |
| **Use for** | Filters, envelopes, saturation, per-note FX | Reverb, delay, EQ, compression, limiting |

**Per-voice processing** means independent state per note. A `PolyphonicFilter` inside a generator gives each voice its own cutoff frequency and filter state. Play a chord — each note gets its own filter sweep, its own resonance response, its own envelope-modulated movement. With 16 active voices, that filter runs 16 times per buffer.

**Master processing** means shared processing on the sum. A `SimpleReverb` on the master chain receives the combined audio from all voices and creates one shared reverb tail. All notes contribute to the same acoustic space. The reverb runs once regardless of how many voices play.

Making this decision wrong doesn't just waste CPU — it changes your sound:

- **Reverbs and delays belong on the master chain.** They create shared time-based spaces. Running a reverb per-voice would create independent reverb tails that don't interact — acoustically wrong and extremely expensive.
- **Filters and saturation belong per-voice.** A master-level filter can't give each note a different cutoff. Per-voice placement gives you independent, modulatable filtering per note.
- **Limiters always go on the master.** They need to see the final summed level to prevent clipping.

A master-level filter produces a fundamentally different result from per-voice filtering. Choose placement based on what the sound design requires.


## Modulation in the Signal Flow

The per-voice rendering stage mentions gain and pitch modulation calculating before the generator renders. Here's what that actually means.

Every generator has two modulation chains — `GainModulation` and `PitchModulation` — where you stack modulators. These modulators run every audio buffer, producing a stream of values that shape the generator's output in real time. They're not one-shot events; they're continuous, per-voice signal processors that output control data rather than audio.

### The Three Modulator Types

| Type | Fires | Output | Examples |
|------|-------|--------|----------|
| **VoiceStartModulator** | Once, when the voice starts | Single fixed value for the voice's lifetime | `Velocity`, `Random`, `KeyNumber` |
| **TimeVariantModulator** | Every buffer, continuously | Changing value over time | `LFO`, `MidiController`, `PitchWheel` |
| **EnvelopeModulator** | Every buffer, per voice | Per-voice shape over time (attack/decay/sustain/release) | `AhdsrEnvelope`, `SimpleEnvelope` |

`Velocity` fires once per note and sets a fixed amplitude scaling — quiet notes stay quiet. An `LFO` on the pitch chain produces continuous vibrato. An `AhdsrEnvelope` on the gain chain shapes each note's amplitude contour — attack, sustain, release.

### How Modulators Stack

Multiple modulators in the same chain combine automatically:

- **GainModulation**: modulators **multiply** together. An `AhdsrEnvelope` at 0.8 × a `Velocity` at 0.5 = 0.4 final gain. Any single modulator reaching zero silences the voice entirely.
- **PitchModulation**: modulators **add** together. An `LFO` vibrato of ±50 cents + a `PitchWheel` bend of +200 cents = vibrato centered around +200 cents. Modulators layer independently.

### Standard Routing Patterns

These patterns appear in virtually every HISE project:

| Modulator → Chain | Effect | Why |
|-------------------|--------|-----|
| `AhdsrEnvelope` → GainModulation | Amplitude envelope | Shapes note volume over time — the most fundamental modulation |
| `Velocity` → GainModulation | Dynamic response | Harder playing = louder |
| `LFO` → PitchModulation | Vibrato | Continuous pitch movement |
| `MidiController` → GainModulation | Expression (CC11) | Real-time volume control from hardware |
| `PitchWheel` → PitchModulation | Pitch bend | Maps pitch wheel to tuning offset |

For deeper coverage — `GlobalModulatorContainer` for shared modulation sources, the `ModulationMatrix` for user-configurable routing, and advanced patterns — see [The Modulation System](/v2/architecture/modulation-system).


## Voice Lifecycle

Every voice moves through a predictable lifecycle from creation to cleanup:

![Voice lifecycle from note-on through release to cleanup](/images/v2/architecture/signal-flow-voice-lifecycle.svg)

1. **Allocation** — a `noteOn` message creates a voice object. The voice joins the active voice list and begins rendering audio.
2. **Active rendering** — the voice renders audio every buffer. Gain and pitch modulators shape its output continuously. This continues as long as the note is held.
3. **Release** — a `noteOff` triggers the `AhdsrEnvelope` release phase. The voice **keeps rendering** — it still produces audio during the release tail. This is why you hear notes fade out instead of cutting off abruptly.
4. **Cleanup** — when the envelope reaches zero (release phase complete), the voice is marked for removal. The next buffer removes it from the active list and returns it to the pool for reuse.

### Voice Stealing

Each generator has a `VoiceLimit` parameter that controls how many voices can play simultaneously. When a new note arrives and no voices are free, **voice stealing** kicks in:

1. The oldest voice (preferring voices already in release) is selected for stealing
2. That voice fades out over `KillFadeTime` milliseconds — a very short crossfade to avoid clicks
3. The freed voice is immediately reused for the new note

Shorter `AhdsrEnvelope` release times free voices faster, reducing the chance of stealing. Higher `VoiceLimit` values allow more simultaneous notes but increase CPU proportionally — every active voice runs the full per-voice pipeline.

**The CPU equation is straightforward:** active voices × per-voice processing cost = total per-voice CPU. A per-voice `PolyphonicFilter` with 16 active voices costs 16× what a single master filter costs. This is the direct trade-off between sound design flexibility and CPU budget.


## How Containers Shape the Flow

The container a generator sits in determines how its audio combines with siblings:

**SynthChain** renders each child independently and sums their outputs. Two `StreamingSampler` processors in a SynthChain produce audio in parallel — each gets its own MIDI, its own voice allocation, its own per-voice processing. The results add together. This is the pattern for multi-articulation instruments: parallel samplers, one per articulation, with `MidiMuter` controlling which ones receive MIDI.

**SynthGroup** renders children as a single shared voice. One `noteOn` creates one voice across all child generators. This matters for synthesis: two `WavetableSynth` oscillators in a `SynthGroup` play together as one note, sharing voice allocation and enabling cross-modulation (FM). Without `SynthGroup`, each oscillator would manage its own voices independently.

**EffectChain** processes in strict serial order. Effect 1's output becomes Effect 2's input. The order in the tree IS the processing order — rearranging effects changes the sound. EQ before compression sounds different from compression before EQ.


## What's Next

Signal flow explains **how** your module tree processes audio at runtime — the sequence from MIDI input to final output. Next, understand the scripting layer that adds logic, UI, and control on top of this architecture.

- **Next →** [The UI Model](/v2/architecture/ui-model) — the component system that builds your plugin's interface

- **Build one →** [Building a Sampler](/v2/guide/building-a-sampler) — apply signal flow concepts to a real instrument
- **Build one →** [Building a Synth](/v2/guide/building-a-synth) — apply per-voice architecture to a synthesizer

For deeper coverage — `GlobalModulatorContainer` for shared modulation sources, the `ModulationMatrix` for user-configurable routing, and advanced patterns — see [The Modulation System](/v2/architecture/modulation-system).

text:
Voice Lifecycle

Every voice moves through a predictable lifecycle from creation to cleanup:

![Voice lifecycle from note-on through release to cleanup](/images/v2/architecture/signal-flow-voice-lifecycle.svg)

1. **Allocation** — a `noteOn` message creates a voice object. The voice joins the active voice list and begins rendering audio.
2. **Active rendering** — the voice renders audio every buffer. Gain and pitch modulators shape its output continuously. This continues as long as the note is held.
3. **Release** — a `noteOff` triggers the `AhdsrEnvelope` release phase. The voice **keeps rendering** — it still produces audio during the release tail. This is why you hear notes fade out instead of cutting off abruptly.
4. **Cleanup** — when the envelope reaches zero (release phase complete), the voice is marked for removal. The next buffer removes it from the active list and returns it to the pool for reuse.

### Voice Stealing

Each generator has a `VoiceLimit` parameter that controls how many voices can play simultaneously. When a new note arrives and no voices are free, **voice stealing** kicks in:

1. The oldest voice (preferring voices already in release) is selected for stealing
2. That voice fades out over `KillFadeTime` milliseconds — a very short crossfade to avoid clicks
3. The freed voice is immediately reused for the new note

Shorter `AhdsrEnvelope` release times free voices faster, reducing the chance of stealing. Higher `VoiceLimit` values allow more simultaneous notes but increase CPU proportionally — every active voice runs the full per-voice pipeline.

**The CPU equation is straightforward:** active voices × per-voice processing cost = total per-voice CPU. A per-voice `PolyphonicFilter` with 16 active voices costs 16× what a single master filter costs. This is the direct trade-off between sound design flexibility and CPU budget.

text:
How Containers Shape the Flow

The container a generator sits in determines how its audio combines with siblings:

**SynthChain** renders each child independently and sums their outputs. Two `StreamingSampler` processors in a SynthChain produce audio in parallel — each gets its own MIDI, its own voice allocation, its own per-voice processing. The results add together. This is the pattern for multi-articulation instruments: parallel samplers, one per articulation, with `MidiMuter` controlling which ones receive MIDI.

**SynthGroup** renders children as a single shared voice. One `noteOn` creates one voice across all child generators. This matters for synthesis: two `WavetableSynth` oscillators in a `SynthGroup` play together as one note, sharing voice allocation and enabling cross-modulation (FM). Without `SynthGroup`, each oscillator would manage its own voices independently.

**EffectChain** processes in strict serial order. Effect 1's output becomes Effect 2's input. The order in the tree IS the processing order — rearranging effects changes the sound. EQ before compression sounds different from compression before EQ.

text:
The [module tree](/v2/architecture/module-tree) defines your audio architecture. The UI model defines what your user sees and interacts with. Every HISE plugin has a user interface built with the **Content API** — a set of factory methods that create components like knobs, buttons, panels, and combo boxes. These components connect to the module tree through callbacks and property bindings, forming the bridge between user interaction and audio behavior.

Understanding the UI model means understanding three things: how components are created and configured, how they connect to the audio engine, and how they're styled. This page covers all three — the structural layer. For hands-on painting, drawing commands, and advanced styling techniques, see the [Custom UI Design](/v2/guide/custom-ui) guide.

text:
The Content API

Every HISE interface starts with a single call:

```javascript
Content.makeFrontInterface(900, 600);
```

This designates the current script processor's Content as the main plugin window and sets its size. It must be the first Content call in your interface script's `onInit` callback.

From there, you build the interface by calling factory methods — each one creates a component and returns a reference:

```javascript
const var Cutoff = Content.addKnob("Cutoff", 10, 10);
const var Bypass = Content.addButton("Bypass", 150, 10);
const var Mode   = Content.addComboBox("Mode", 290, 10);
const var Panel1 = Content.addPanel("Panel1", 10, 80);
```

Every factory method takes a unique name and an x/y position. The name is the component's identity — you'll use it to retrieve references, bind properties, and persist preset values. To access a component created elsewhere (or in the Interface Designer), use `Content.getComponent()`:

```javascript
const var Cutoff = Content.getComponent("Cutoff");
```

Always store references as `const var`. The component itself is mutable — you can change its properties, value, and appearance — but the reference binding should never change.

### Static Component Lifetime

This is the most important constraint in HISE's UI model: **all components must be created during `onInit`.** After initialization, the component tree is frozen. You cannot create new sliders, remove existing buttons, or change the number of components at runtime.

The constraint exists because the engine pre-allocates the entire component tree at compile time. Component positions in the tree map directly to preset slots and DAW automation indices. Adding or removing components at runtime would invalidate that mapping, breaking preset recall and automation.

For most plugin UIs this is perfectly fine — a synthesizer's controls don't change while you play. When you do need dynamic UI behavior (scrollable lists, variable-length displays), HISE provides workarounds: `ScriptPanel.addChildPanel()` for creating child panels dynamically, `ScriptedViewport` table mode for data-driven lists, and component preallocation with visibility toggling for switchable layouts. These are covered in [ScriptPanel](#scriptpanel-the-custom-component) below.

### Factory Methods

| Method | Returns | Primary Use |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `Content.addKnob()` | `ScriptSlider` | Rotary knobs and linear sliders |
| `Content.addButton()` | `ScriptButton` | Toggle and momentary buttons |
| `Content.addComboBox()` | `ScriptComboBox` | Dropdown selectors |
| `Content.addPanel()` | `ScriptPanel` | Custom drawing, containers, interactive controls |
| `Content.addLabel()` | `ScriptLabel` | Text display and input |
| `Content.addTable()` | `ScriptTable` | Curve editors (velocity, envelopes) |
| `Content.addSliderPack()` | `ScriptSliderPack` | Multi-slider arrays |
| `Content.addAudioWaveform()` | `ScriptAudioWaveform` | Sample and buffer display |
| `Content.addImage()` | `ScriptImage` | Static and filmstrip images |
| `Content.addViewport()` | `ScriptedViewport` | Scrollable lists and tables |
| `Content.addFloatingTile()` | `ScriptFloatingTile` | Embeds built-in HISE widgets |
| `Content.addWebView()` | `ScriptWebView` | Embedded web content |

text:
Component Types

The six core component types cover the vast majority of plugin interfaces:

| Type | What it does | Modes / Variants |
|------|-------------|------------------|
| **ScriptSlider** | Continuous parameter control | Knob, Horizontal, Vertical, Range |
| **ScriptButton** | Binary on/off control | Toggle, momentary, radio groups |
| **ScriptComboBox** | Selection from a list | Dropdown with string items |
| **ScriptPanel** | Anything custom | Paint routines, mouse input, timers, child panels |
| **ScriptLabel** | Text display or input | Static text, editable text fields |
| **ScriptTable** | Curve editing | Velocity curves, waveshaping, envelope shapes |

`ScriptSlider` is named "Knob" in the factory method but covers all continuous controls — rotary knobs, horizontal sliders, vertical faders, and range sliders, selected via the `mode` property.

`ScriptPanel` is the escape hatch. When no standard component fits — a peak meter, an XY pad, a sequencer grid, a custom waveform display — you build it as a panel with a paint routine and mouse callbacks. It's the most architecturally important component type and gets its own section below.

### Specialized Types

Beyond the core six, HISE provides specialized components for specific data types:

- **ScriptSliderPack** — an array of sliders for multi-value editing (step sequencers, harmonic editors)
- **ScriptAudioWaveform** — waveform display bound to audio buffers or sample data
- **ScriptedViewport** — scrollable container with an optional table mode for dynamic, data-driven lists
- **ScriptFloatingTile** — embeds pre-built HISE widgets (preset browsers, keyboards, analysers)
- **ScriptWebView** — embedded web browser for HTML/JS-based UI elements

### Automatability

Only four component types can be exposed as DAW automation parameters: **ScriptSlider**, **ScriptButton**, **ScriptComboBox**, and **ScriptPanel**. Labels, tables, waveforms, and other display-oriented types cannot be automated — they're for visual feedback or data editing, not single-value parameter control.

text:
Floating Tiles

Floating Tiles are **pre-built, self-contained UI widgets** that you embed into your interface via `Content.addFloatingTile()`. They provide complex features — preset browsing, MIDI keyboards, audio analysers — without custom drawing code.

```javascript
const var PresetTile = Content.addFloatingTile("PresetTile", 0, 0);
PresetTile.set("width", 900);
PresetTile.set("height", 500);

PresetTile.setContentData({
    "Type": "PresetBrowser",
    "Font": "Oxygen Bold",
    "FontSize": 18,
    "ShowFolderButton": false
});
```

Each tile type accepts a JSON configuration object. You set the type, configure its properties, and the tile handles all internal behavior — user interaction, data management, and rendering.

Key Floating Tile types:

| Category | Types |
|----------|-------|
| **Presets & Settings** | `PresetBrowser`, `CustomSettings`, `MidiLearnPanel` |
| **Keyboard & MIDI** | `Keyboard`, `MidiSources`, `MidiChannelList`, `MPEPanel` |
| **Visualizers** | `AudioAnalyser`, `FilterGraph`, `DraggableFilterPanel`, `Plotter` |
| **Envelopes** | `AHDSRGraph`, `FlexAHDSRGraph` |
| **Meters & Status** | `MatrixPeakMeter`, `PerformanceLabel`, `ActivityLed` |
| **Content** | `MarkdownPanel`, `TooltipPanel`, `AboutPagePanel` |
| **Modulation** | `ModulationMatrix`, `ModulationMatrixController` |

`PresetBrowser` is the most commonly used — it provides a three-column browser (bank / category / preset) with search, favorites, and save/delete functionality out of the box. Floating Tiles can be styled with the Look and Feel system — functions like `drawPresetBrowserListItem` and `drawWhiteNote` let you customize their appearance to match your plugin's design.

text: How component state persists — saveInPreset, user presets, DAW automation, and DefaultUserPreset
body:
The [UI model](/v2/architecture/ui-model) creates components. The data model defines what happens to their values — how they're saved, restored, and exposed to the DAW. HISE's answer is a direct coupling: **a UI component is a preset slot is an automation parameter**. Declaring a knob with the right properties simultaneously declares a value that persists across presets and DAW sessions, with zero serialization code.

This coupling is one of HISE's most distinctive design decisions. Understanding it explains why presets "just work" in every HISE project and why `saveInPreset` is the single most consequential component property.

The [UI model](/v2/architecture/ui-model) creates components. The data model defines what happens to their values — how they're saved, restored, and exposed to the DAW. HISE's answer is a direct coupling: **a UI component is a preset slot is an automation parameter**. Declaring a knob with the right properties simultaneously declares a value that persists across presets and DAW sessions, with zero serialization code.

This coupling is one of HISE's most distinctive design decisions. Understanding it explains why presets "just work" in every HISE project and why `saveInPreset` is the single most consequential component property.
