text: Parameter connections, the Broadcaster event system, and how data flows through a HISE project
body:
The [scripting model](/v2/architecture/scripting-model) shows how scripts reference modules and wire UI callbacks. The [UI model](/v2/architecture/ui-model) shows how components bind directly to parameters through properties. The [data model](/v2/architecture/data-model) shows how component values persist across presets and DAW sessions. This page ties all three together: how data flows between user interaction, UI components, scripts, and the audio engine — and the three connection tiers HISE provides, from zero-code property bindings to a full reactive event system.


## The Connection Tiers

HISE provides three mechanisms for connecting UI components to the audio engine, each adding capability and complexity. This is the **escalation path** — start with the simplest mechanism that works, and step up only when you need more power.

| Tier | Mechanism | What It Does | Use When |
|------|-----------|-------------|----------|
| 1 | `processorId` / `parameterId` | Zero-code 1:1 binding. Set two component properties and the connection is automatic and bidirectional. | A knob maps directly to one parameter with no logic. |
| 2 | `setControlCallback` | An inline function fires when the component value changes. Full scripting power. | You need math, conditions, or one knob controlling multiple parameters. |
| 3 | Broadcaster | A reactive event bus. Sources detect changes, targets react. Decoupled, scalable, debuggable. | Multiple listeners need to react to one event, or state must synchronize across components. |

The tiers aren't competing alternatives — they're complementary. Most shipping instruments use all three simultaneously: Tier 1 for the 20 knobs that map directly to parameters, Tier 2 for the 5–8 knobs that need arithmetic or multi-target routing, and Tier 3 for cross-cutting concerns like page switching, preset lifecycle hooks, and coordinated parameter updates.

<!-- SVG: data-flow-escalation-path.svg — Three tiers stacked vertically, increasing in capability. Tier 1: single straight arrow from "UI Component" to "Module Parameter", labeled "processorId". Tier 2: arrow from "UI Component" through an "inline function" box to "Module Parameter", labeled "setControlCallback". Tier 3: multiple source arrows entering a "Broadcaster" hub, multiple target arrows leaving to different destinations (component property, component value, module parameter, custom function). Annotate left axis with "complexity" (low → high), right axis with "power" (low → high). Use dark panels (#353535) for boxes, HISE green (#78be8a) for the active connection arrows, light text (#E0E0E0). -->

### Tier 1: Property Binding

Set `processorId` and `parameterId` on a UI component, and HISE wires the connection automatically — no script code needed. The component controls the parameter, DAW automation updates the component, and preset recall restores the value. The binding is bidirectional: changes from either side stay in sync.

This is the right default. The Connection Wizard in the IDE automates the property assignment. Switch to Tier 2 only when you need logic that a direct binding can't express.

See [The UI Model — Zero-Code Parameter Binding](/v2/architecture/ui-model#zero-code-parameter-binding) for details and code examples.

### Tier 2: Control Callbacks

When a connection needs logic — scaling a value, controlling multiple parameters from one knob, or applying conditions — register an inline function with `setControlCallback`. The function receives the component and its new value. Inside, you call `setAttribute` on one or more module references to translate user interaction into audio changes.

This is the workhorse for connections that need scripted intelligence. One callback can update a filter frequency, adjust a linked resonance value, and refresh a display label. But each callback is wired to one component, and if multiple components need to trigger the same logic, you start writing coordination code.

See [The Scripting Model — setControlCallback](/v2/architecture/scripting-model#setcontrolcallback) for details, code examples, and the grouped callback pattern.

### Tier 3: Broadcaster

When one event needs to reach multiple independent targets — or when you need to decouple the source of a change from its effects — the Broadcaster system provides a reactive publish-subscribe model. This is HISE's most powerful connection mechanism, and the one that separates small projects from scalable architectures.

The rest of this page focuses on Tier 3 and the overall data flow picture it enables.


## The Component as Data Junction

Before diving into Broadcasters, it helps to see the architectural role UI components play in HISE's data flow. A component isn't just a visual element — it's the **central junction** between four systems:

| System | How It Interacts With the Component |
|--------|-------------------------------------|
| **User** | Turns a knob, clicks a button → component value changes |
| **Presets** | Loading a `.preset` file → all `saveInPreset` components restored to saved values |
| **DAW** | Moving an automation lane → `isPluginParameter` components updated |
| **Script** | Calling `setValue()` / `getValue()` → reads or writes component state programmatically |

From the component, data flows outward into the module tree through whichever connection tier is wired — `processorId` binding, `setControlCallback`, or a Broadcaster target calling `setAttribute`. This is the **forward path**: user interaction becomes audio change.

The **reverse path** matters equally. When a module parameter changes from outside the script — through DAW automation, preset loading, or a different script — the UI needs to reflect that change. Tier 1 bindings handle this automatically (they're bidirectional). For Tier 2, the callback fires whenever the component value changes, regardless of whether the user or the system triggered it. Broadcasters can watch module parameters directly via `attachToModuleParameter`, catching changes from any source and routing them to any number of UI targets.

<!-- SVG: data-flow-project-overview.svg — The complete data flow picture. Center: large "UI Component" box (use #E4E4E4 with dark text). Four arrows entering from the left/top: "User Interaction", "Preset Load" (saveInPreset), "DAW Automation" (isPluginParameter), "Script" (setValue). One main arrow leaving right/bottom to "Module Tree → Audio Engine" box (use #353535 with light text), labeled with the three tier names along the arrow. A return arrow from Module Tree back to UI Component labeled "Broadcaster (attachToModuleParameter)" or "processorId (bidirectional)". Use HISE green (#78be8a) for the forward-path arrow, #909090 for the reverse-path arrow. -->

This centrality of the component layer explains several HISE design decisions. Adding a knob automatically creates a preset slot *and* a potential automation parameter — because the component IS the data junction, not just a visual control. Preset loading fires callbacks — because it changes component values, which flow through the same paths as user interaction. The [data model](/v2/architecture/data-model)'s `saveInPreset` coupling isn't a convenience feature — it's a direct consequence of components being the canonical state holders.


## The Broadcaster System

For small projects, `setControlCallback` handles every connection comfortably. But as instruments grow, direct callbacks create pressure points.

**Fan-out.** One state change needs to update 5+ UI components — the callback grows into a monolith that knows about every target. Adding a sixth target means editing the same callback again.

**Reverse notification.** A module parameter changes from DAW automation or another script — there's no built-in way for a `setControlCallback` to detect this. You'd need to poll.

**Cross-cutting state.** Page switching needs to coordinate 20+ component visibility states. Preset loading needs to trigger side effects in a specific order. A radio group needs to sync across multiple UI sections. All require manual orchestration that lives outside the natural callback structure.

**Debugging.** When a UI element doesn't update correctly, you trace through nested callbacks with no visibility into the overall data flow graph. The problem could be anywhere in the chain.

The Broadcaster solves these problems by bringing **publish-subscribe** into the script layer.

### Sources, Broadcaster, Targets

A Broadcaster is a **named message bus** with two sides:

```
[Sources]  →  [Broadcaster]  →  [Targets]
  (detect)     (named bus)       (react)
```

**Sources** detect changes and feed events into the Broadcaster. They're attached with `attachTo*()` methods — each method watches a different type of event. A single Broadcaster can have multiple sources.

**Targets** react when the Broadcaster fires. They're registered with `addListener()` and specialized add methods. A single Broadcaster can have multiple targets.

The Broadcaster itself holds the **current state** — the last set of argument values that passed through it. This means a target attached after the initial event can request the current state via `resendLastMessage` without waiting for the next change. The Broadcaster is stateful, not just a fire-and-forget pipe.

### Source Types

Around 15 source types cover the events a script might need to react to:

| Category | What It Detects |
|----------|----------------|
| **Component values** | Value changes on knobs, buttons, combo boxes |
| **Component properties** | Changes to text, color, visibility, or any named property |
| **Component interaction** | Mouse clicks, drags, hovers on specific components |
| **Radio groups** | Button selection within a numbered radio group |
| **Module parameters** | Processor parameter changes — from user, DAW, preset, or script |
| **Complex data** | AudioFile, SliderPack, or Table content changes |
| **EQ events** | EQ band added, removed, selected, or FFT toggled |
| **Sample map events** | Sample map changes, sample property edits |
| **System events** | Sample rate, block size, interface size, routing matrix changes |
| **Other Broadcasters** | Messages from another Broadcaster — enabling reactive chains |

Each source type determines the **argument signature** of the Broadcaster. A component-value source provides `(component, value)`. A module-parameter source provides `(processorId, parameterId, value)`. Sources and targets must agree on the argument count and meaning.

### Target Types

Targets determine what happens when the Broadcaster fires:

| Target | What It Does |
|--------|-------------|
| **General listener** | Calls an inline function with the Broadcaster's arguments — full scripting flexibility |
| **Component property listener** | Sets properties (text, color, visibility) on components, with an optional transform function |
| **Component value listener** | Sets the value of components, optionally transformed |
| **Component refresh listener** | Triggers a repaint, value update, or focus reset on components |
| **Module parameter syncer** | Directly syncs a module parameter to the source value — forces synchronous execution [VERIFY] |

The combination of typed sources and typed targets means many common patterns require **no custom callback code at all**. A Broadcaster that watches a knob's value and syncs it to a label's text property can be wired entirely through source and target type declarations — the plumbing is handled by the system.

<!-- SVG: data-flow-broadcaster-architecture.svg — A concrete example of the two-sided architecture. Left side: "knobFilter" component box (source, use #E4E4E4 with dark text). Arrow labeled "attachToComponentValue" pointing to center: "filterFrequency" Broadcaster hub (use #353535 with light text, HISE green #78be8a border). Two arrows leaving right: one labeled "addComponentPropertyListener" pointing to "lblFreq" component box (#E4E4E4), one labeled "addListener → setAttribute" pointing to "filter.Frequency" module parameter box (use FX color #386464 with light text). Clean, schematic, generous spacing. -->

### In Practice

One Broadcaster replacing what would otherwise be a `setControlCallback` with manual label updates and parameter wiring:

```javascript
// Module reference (established in onInit)
const var filter = Synth.getEffect("PolyphonicFilter");

// Create a Broadcaster with a component-value argument signature
const var filterBC = Engine.createBroadcaster({
    id: "filterFrequency",
    args: ["component", "value"]
});

// Source: watch the filter knob's value
filterBC.attachToComponentValue("knobFilter", "");

// Target 1: update the frequency display label
filterBC.addComponentPropertyListener(["lblFreq"], ["text"], "",
    function(index, component, property, value)
    {
        return Math.round(value) + " Hz";
    });

// Target 2: set the filter module's frequency parameter
filterBC.addListener(0, "setFilterParam",
    function(component, value)
    {
        filter.setAttribute(filter.Frequency, value);
    });
```

Either target can be added, removed, or replaced independently. Adding a third target — say, a visual filter curve that repaints when the frequency changes — is one `addComponentRefreshListener` call. No existing code needs to change. This is the architectural advantage: **each concern is a separate target, not a line inside a growing callback function.**

### Design Properties

The Broadcaster system is built for the realities of shipping instruments:

- **Decoupled.** Sources don't know about targets. Adding or removing either side doesn't affect the other. This is what makes Broadcasters scale — a new UI panel can subscribe to existing Broadcasters without touching the code that fires them.
- **Named and debuggable.** Every Broadcaster carries an ID and optional metadata — a comment, a display color, priority ordering, and tags. The Broadcaster Map (below) uses this metadata to render the entire event topology as a visual graph.
- **Synchronous or asynchronous.** `sendSyncMessage` for timing-critical updates, `sendAsyncMessage` for batched UI-safe delivery. Configurable per-Broadcaster, with a force-synchronous option for cases where timing guarantees matter.
- **Bypassable.** Temporarily disable a Broadcaster with `setBypassed` — useful for suppressing cascade updates during batch operations like preset loading.
- **Stateful.** The Broadcaster remembers its last argument values. Late-attached targets can call `resendLastMessage` to receive the current state immediately, without waiting for the next change event.

For decision frameworks on choosing between the three connection tiers, practical Broadcaster wiring patterns, and debugging workflows, see [Events & Messaging](/v2/guide/events-and-messaging).


## The Broadcaster Map

HISE includes a visual debugging tool for Broadcaster-based architectures: the **Broadcaster Map**. It renders every Broadcaster in the current project as a node graph, showing all Broadcasters with their IDs, all attached sources with their types, all registered targets with their metadata, and the connections between them.

For projects using Tier 3 connections, the Broadcaster Map answers "what happens when this knob changes?" without tracing through script files. It turns an invisible event graph into a visible, inspectable topology — and it's one of the architectural advantages of the Broadcaster system over direct callback chains, where data flow is implicit in control flow and can only be traced by reading code.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: The Broadcaster Map panel showing a small project's event topology — a few Broadcasters with sources and targets connected as a node graph -->

[VERIFY: Is the Broadcaster Map accessed through a specific menu path or panel? Is it a stable feature in current HISE builds?]


## DSP Network Connections

The three connection tiers above operate within the script layer — they connect UI components, script logic, and module tree parameters. But [scriptnode DSP networks](/v2/architecture/scriptnode) run in a separate domain. When a DSP network needs to communicate with the script layer — sending peak levels to a meter, receiving toggle states from a button, or exposing internal state for visual feedback — HISE provides **GlobalRoutingManager cables**: named point-to-point connections that bridge the DSP and script domains.

Unlike Broadcasters, routing cables are not pub-sub — they're direct, named channels designed for the specific case of DSP ↔ script communication. They complement the Broadcaster system rather than replacing it: use Broadcasters for script-layer event routing, and routing cables when a DSP network needs to participate in the data flow.

[VERIFY: Is "GlobalRoutingManager" the correct user-facing name, or is this an internal API? How are cables created from HiseScript? Should this section live here or in the Scriptnode architecture page?]


## Patterns from Real Projects

Production instruments combine the connection tiers into recognizable architectural patterns:

**Mixed-tier (most common).** A typical shipping instrument uses `processorId` bindings for 15–25 straightforward knobs, `setControlCallback` for 5–10 knobs that need scaling or conditional logic, and 3–5 Broadcasters for page state, preset lifecycle hooks, and coordinated parameter groups. This mixed approach isn't a compromise — it's the intended design. Each tier handles the connections it's best suited for.

**Hub-and-spoke (large instruments).** Projects with complex state centralize their Broadcasters in a dedicated script namespace — a "data globals" module that acts as the event backbone. All UI modules and script logic subscribe to these central Broadcasters rather than having direct dependencies on each other. This creates clean separation between data flow and rendering, and makes the Broadcaster Map immediately useful for understanding the architecture.

**Chained Broadcasters (advanced).** Broadcasters can watch other Broadcasters via `attachToOtherBroadcaster`, creating reactive chains with optional argument transformation. A preset-load Broadcaster fires → a UI-refresh Broadcaster catches it and triggers component updates → individual display Broadcasters repaint specific panels. Each Broadcaster in the chain handles one concern, making complex lifecycle management traceable and debuggable.

For code examples of these patterns — EQ parameter coordination, drag-bypass interaction, state bus architecture, and more — see [Broadcaster Patterns](/v2/examples/broadcaster-patterns).


## What's Next

The connection tiers and data flow model complete the architectural picture of how user interaction becomes audio behavior in HISE.

- **Deep dive →** [Events & Messaging](/v2/guide/events-and-messaging) — decision frameworks for choosing between tiers, practical Broadcaster wiring patterns with code, and debugging workflows
- **Patterns →** [Broadcaster Patterns](/v2/examples/broadcaster-patterns) — six named reactive patterns from production projects, with code examples
- **Related →** [The Scripting Model](/v2/architecture/scripting-model) — `setControlCallback`, module references, and the five callback slots
- **Related →** [The UI Model](/v2/architecture/ui-model) — `processorId` binding, component types, and the Interface Designer
- **Related →** [Data Model & Presets](/v2/architecture/data-model) — `saveInPreset`, the preset lifecycle, and DAW automation

|------|-----------|-------------|----------|

text:
The Component as Data Junction

Before diving into Broadcasters, it helps to see the architectural role UI components play in HISE's data flow. A component isn't just a visual element — it's the **central junction** between four systems:

| System | How It Interacts With the Component |
|--------|-------------------------------------|
| **User** | Turns a knob, clicks a button → component value changes |
| **Presets** | Loading a `.preset` file → all `saveInPreset` components restored to saved values |
| **DAW** | Moving an automation lane → `isPluginParameter` components updated |
| **Script** | Calling `setValue()` / `getValue()` → reads or writes component state programmatically |

From the component, data flows outward into the module tree through whichever connection tier is wired — `processorId` binding, `setControlCallback`, or a Broadcaster target calling `setAttribute`. This is the **forward path**: user interaction becomes audio change.

The **reverse path** matters equally. When a module parameter changes from outside the script — through DAW automation, preset loading, or a different script — the UI needs to reflect that change. Tier 1 bindings handle this automatically (they're bidirectional). For Tier 2, the callback fires whenever the component value changes, regardless of whether the user or the system triggered it. Broadcasters can watch module parameters directly via `attachToModuleParameter`, catching changes from any source and routing them to any number of UI targets.

<!-- SVG: data-flow-project-overview.svg — The complete data flow picture. Center: large "UI Component" box (use #E4E4E4 with dark text). Four arrows entering from the left/top: "User Interaction", "Preset Load" (saveInPreset), "DAW Automation" (isPluginParameter), "Script" (setValue). One main arrow leaving right/bottom to "Module Tree → Audio Engine" box (use #353535 with light text), labeled with the three tier names along the arrow. A return arrow from Module Tree back to UI Component labeled "Broadcaster (attachToModuleParameter)" or "processorId (bidirectional)". Use HISE green (#78be8a) for the forward-path arrow, #909090 for the reverse-path arrow. -->

This centrality of the component layer explains several HISE design decisions. Adding a knob automatically creates a preset slot *and* a potential automation parameter — because the component IS the data junction, not just a visual control. Preset loading fires callbacks — because it changes component values, which flow through the same paths as user interaction. The [data model](/v2/architecture/data-model)'s `saveInPreset` coupling isn't a convenience feature — it's a direct consequence of components being the canonical state holders.

text:
The Broadcaster System

For small projects, `setControlCallback` handles every connection comfortably. But as instruments grow, direct callbacks create pressure points.

**Fan-out.** One state change needs to update 5+ UI components — the callback grows into a monolith that knows about every target. Adding a sixth target means editing the same callback again.

**Reverse notification.** A module parameter changes from DAW automation or another script — there's no built-in way for a `setControlCallback` to detect this. You'd need to poll.

**Cross-cutting state.** Page switching needs to coordinate 20+ component visibility states. Preset loading needs to trigger side effects in a specific order. A radio group needs to sync across multiple UI sections. All require manual orchestration that lives outside the natural callback structure.

**Debugging.** When a UI element doesn't update correctly, you trace through nested callbacks with no visibility into the overall data flow graph. The problem could be anywhere in the chain.

The Broadcaster solves these problems by bringing **publish-subscribe** into the script layer.

### Sources, Broadcaster, Targets

A Broadcaster is a **named message bus** with two sides:

```
[Sources]  →  [Broadcaster]  →  [Targets]
  (detect)     (named bus)       (react)
```

**Sources** detect changes and feed events into the Broadcaster. They're attached with `attachTo*()` methods — each method watches a different type of event. A single Broadcaster can have multiple sources.

**Targets** react when the Broadcaster fires. They're registered with `addListener()` and specialized add methods. A single Broadcaster can have multiple targets.

The Broadcaster itself holds the **current state** — the last set of argument values that passed through it. This means a target attached after the initial event can request the current state via `resendLastMessage` without waiting for the next change. The Broadcaster is stateful, not just a fire-and-forget pipe.

### Source Types

Around 15 source types cover the events a script might need to react to:

| Category | What It Detects |
|----------|----------------|
| **Component values** | Value changes on knobs, buttons, combo boxes |
| **Component properties** | Changes to text, color, visibility, or any named property |
| **Component interaction** | Mouse clicks, drags, hovers on specific components |
| **Radio groups** | Button selection within a numbered radio group |
| **Module parameters** | Processor parameter changes — from user, DAW, preset, or script |
| **Complex data** | AudioFile, SliderPack, or Table content changes |
| **EQ events** | EQ band added, removed, selected, or FFT toggled |
| **Sample map events** | Sample map changes, sample property edits |
| **System events** | Sample rate, block size, interface size, routing matrix changes |
| **Other Broadcasters** | Messages from another Broadcaster — enabling reactive chains |

Each source type determines the **argument signature** of the Broadcaster. A component-value source provides `(component, value)`. A module-parameter source provides `(processorId, parameterId, value)`. Sources and targets must agree on the argument count and meaning.

### Target Types

Targets determine what happens when the Broadcaster fires:

| Target | What It Does |
|--------|-------------|
| **General listener** | Calls an inline function with the Broadcaster's arguments — full scripting flexibility |
| **Component property listener** | Sets properties (text, color, visibility) on components, with an optional transform function |
| **Component value listener** | Sets the value of components, optionally transformed |
| **Component refresh listener** | Triggers a repaint, value update, or focus reset on components |
| **Module parameter syncer** | Directly syncs a module parameter to the source value — forces synchronous execution [VERIFY] |

The combination of typed sources and typed targets means many common patterns require **no custom callback code at all**. A Broadcaster that watches a knob's value and syncs it to a label's text property can be wired entirely through source and target type declarations — the plumbing is handled by the system.

<!-- SVG: data-flow-broadcaster-architecture.svg — A concrete example of the two-sided architecture. Left side: "knobFilter" component box (source, use #E4E4E4 with dark text). Arrow labeled "attachToComponentValue" pointing to center: "filterFrequency" Broadcaster hub (use #353535 with light text, HISE green #78be8a border). Two arrows leaving right: one labeled "addComponentPropertyListener" pointing to "lblFreq" component box (#E4E4E4), one labeled "addListener → setAttribute" pointing to "filter.Frequency" module parameter box (use FX color #386464 with light text). Clean, schematic, generous spacing. -->

### In Practice

One Broadcaster replacing what would otherwise be a `setControlCallback` with manual label updates and parameter wiring:

```javascript
// Module reference (established in onInit)
const var filter = Synth.getEffect("PolyphonicFilter");

// Create a Broadcaster with a component-value argument signature
const var filterBC = Engine.createBroadcaster({
    id: "filterFrequency",
    args: ["component", "value"]
});

// Source: watch the filter knob's value
filterBC.attachToComponentValue("knobFilter", "");

// Target 1: update the frequency display label
filterBC.addComponentPropertyListener(["lblFreq"], ["text"], "",
    function(index, component, property, value)
    {
        return Math.round(value) + " Hz";
    });

// Target 2: set the filter module's frequency parameter
filterBC.addListener(0, "setFilterParam",
    function(component, value)
    {
        filter.setAttribute(filter.Frequency, value);
    });
```

Either target can be added, removed, or replaced independently. Adding a third target — say, a visual filter curve that repaints when the frequency changes — is one `addComponentRefreshListener` call. No existing code needs to change. This is the architectural advantage: **each concern is a separate target, not a line inside a growing callback function.**

### Design Properties

The Broadcaster system is built for the realities of shipping instruments:

- **Decoupled.** Sources don't know about targets. Adding or removing either side doesn't affect the other. This is what makes Broadcasters scale — a new UI panel can subscribe to existing Broadcasters without touching the code that fires them.
- **Named and debuggable.** Every Broadcaster carries an ID and optional metadata — a comment, a display color, priority ordering, and tags. The Broadcaster Map (below) uses this metadata to render the entire event topology as a visual graph.
- **Synchronous or asynchronous.** `sendSyncMessage` for timing-critical updates, `sendAsyncMessage` for batched UI-safe delivery. Configurable per-Broadcaster, with a force-synchronous option for cases where timing guarantees matter.
- **Bypassable.** Temporarily disable a Broadcaster with `setBypassed` — useful for suppressing cascade updates during batch operations like preset loading.
- **Stateful.** The Broadcaster remembers its last argument values. Late-attached targets can call `resendLastMessage` to receive the current state immediately, without waiting for the next change event.

For decision frameworks on choosing between the three connection tiers, practical Broadcaster wiring patterns, and debugging workflows, see [Events & Messaging](/v2/guide/events-and-messaging).

text:
The Broadcaster Map

HISE includes a visual debugging tool for Broadcaster-based architectures: the **Broadcaster Map**. It renders every Broadcaster in the current project as a node graph, showing all Broadcasters with their IDs, all attached sources with their types, all registered targets with their metadata, and the connections between them.

For projects using Tier 3 connections, the Broadcaster Map answers "what happens when this knob changes?" without tracing through script files. It turns an invisible event graph into a visible, inspectable topology — and it's one of the architectural advantages of the Broadcaster system over direct callback chains, where data flow is implicit in control flow and can only be traced by reading code.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: The Broadcaster Map panel showing a small project's event topology — a few Broadcasters with sources and targets connected as a node graph -->

text:
DSP Network Connections

The three connection tiers above operate within the script layer — they connect UI components, script logic, and module tree parameters. But [scriptnode DSP networks](/v2/architecture/scriptnode) run in a separate domain. When a DSP network needs to communicate with the script layer — sending peak levels to a meter, receiving toggle states from a button, or exposing internal state for visual feedback — HISE provides **GlobalRoutingManager cables**: named point-to-point connections that bridge the DSP and script domains.

Unlike Broadcasters, routing cables are not pub-sub — they're direct, named channels designed for the specific case of DSP ↔ script communication. They complement the Broadcaster system rather than replacing it: use Broadcasters for script-layer event routing, and routing cables when a DSP network needs to participate in the data flow.

text:
Patterns from Real Projects

Production instruments combine the connection tiers into recognizable architectural patterns:

**Mixed-tier (most common).** A typical shipping instrument uses `processorId` bindings for 15–25 straightforward knobs, `setControlCallback` for 5–10 knobs that need scaling or conditional logic, and 3–5 Broadcasters for page state, preset lifecycle hooks, and coordinated parameter groups. This mixed approach isn't a compromise — it's the intended design. Each tier handles the connections it's best suited for.

**Hub-and-spoke (large instruments).** Projects with complex state centralize their Broadcasters in a dedicated script namespace — a "data globals" module that acts as the event backbone. All UI modules and script logic subscribe to these central Broadcasters rather than having direct dependencies on each other. This creates clean separation between data flow and rendering, and makes the Broadcaster Map immediately useful for understanding the architecture.

**Chained Broadcasters (advanced).** Broadcasters can watch other Broadcasters via `attachToOtherBroadcaster`, creating reactive chains with optional argument transformation. A preset-load Broadcaster fires → a UI-refresh Broadcaster catches it and triggers component updates → individual display Broadcasters repaint specific panels. Each Broadcaster in the chain handles one concern, making complex lifecycle management traceable and debuggable.

For code examples of these patterns — EQ parameter coordination, drag-bypass interaction, state bus architecture, and more — see [Broadcaster Patterns](/v2/examples/broadcaster-patterns).

text: Node-based DSP graphs, container types, the three DSP tiers, and the compilation pipeline
body:
The [module tree](/v2/architecture/module-tree) provides built-in processors for common tasks — reverbs, filters, delays, EQ. But some projects need DSP that doesn't exist as a built-in module: a custom filter topology, a granular engine, a Faust reverb algorithm. That's where **scriptnode** comes in.

Scriptnode is HISE's visual, node-based DSP system. You build signal processing graphs by connecting nodes in a visual editor, expose parameters to the script layer, and optionally compile the whole network to C++ for production performance. It's the second of HISE's [three DSP tiers](/v2/architecture/overview) — more flexible than built-in modules, less effort than writing raw C++.

This page covers the concepts. For hands-on network building, see [Building DSP Networks](/v2/guide/dsp-networks).

<!-- TODO: Phase 2 content -->
<!-- This is a SPECIAL page — multiple sections of ~1000w each -->
<!-- Focus: FX archetype (effect plugins are the primary scriptnode users) -->

## What Scriptnode Is

<!-- TODO: (~1000w) -->
<!--   - A DSP network is a graph of nodes that process audio -->
<!--   - Networks are stored as XML in DspNetworks/Networks/ -->
<!--   - Hosted in the module tree by HardcodedMasterFX (master) or HardcodedPolyphonicFX (per-voice) -->
<!--   - The scriptnode editor: visual patching, real-time parameter tweaking -->
<!--   - Networks have parameters that scripts can control via setAttribute -->
<!--   - When to reach for scriptnode: -->
<!--     - Custom filter topologies, MS encoding, multi-band splits -->
<!--     - Faust algorithms (reverbs, resonators, waveguides) -->
<!--     - Complex parameter routing (cable_expr transformations) -->
<!--     - Any DSP that built-in modules can't do -->
<!--   - When NOT to: if a built-in module exists, use it (simpler, no compilation step) -->

## Container Types

<!-- TODO: (~1000w) -->
<!--   - container.chain — serial: output of node 1 → input of node 2 -->
<!--   - container.split — parallel: input duplicated to N paths, outputs summed -->
<!--   - container.multi — multi-channel: each channel processed independently -->
<!--   - container.frame — per-sample: process one sample at a time (for feedback, state) -->
<!--   - container.oversample — oversampled processing (2x, 4x, 8x, 16x) -->
<!--   - container.soft_bypass — bypassable sub-graph with crossfade -->
<!--   - TABLE: container types, when to use each -->
<!--   - Nesting: containers inside containers for complex routing -->
<!--   - Example: MS processing = split → LR2MS → mid chain / side chain → MS2LR → sum -->

## The Three DSP Tiers

<!-- TODO: (~800w) -->
<!--   - Tier 1: Built-in HISE modules (drag-and-drop in module tree) -->
<!--     - SimpleReverb, Convolution, PolyphonicFilter, Delay, CurveEq, etc. -->
<!--     - Covers most needs — 4/13 analyzed projects use no scriptnode -->
<!--   - Tier 2: Scriptnode stock nodes + Faust -->
<!--     - ~100 stock nodes: core.gain, core.oscillator, math.mul, control.cable_expr, etc. -->
<!--     - Faust integration: write Faust DSP code, compile to a scriptnode node -->
<!--     - Visual patching in the scriptnode editor -->
<!--   - Tier 3: Custom C++ / Faust ThirdParty nodes -->
<!--     - C++ header files in DspNetworks/ThirdParty/ -->
<!--     - Full control over the DSP algorithm -->
<!--     - For novel algorithms and performance-critical paths -->
<!--   - TABLE: tiers with flexibility, effort, and use cases -->
<!--   - Start at Tier 1. Escalate when you hit its limits. -->

## The Compilation Pipeline

<!-- TODO: (~600w) -->
<!--   - Design phase: build and test in the scriptnode editor (interpreted, real-time) -->
<!--   - Export: network XML → C++ source generation → compile with project -->
<!--   - Result: HardcodedMasterFX / HardcodedPolyphonicFX with native performance -->
<!--   - Why compile: interpreted scriptnode is fine for development but compiled = production -->
<!--   - The workflow: design → test → freeze → compile → ship -->
<!--   - ThirdParty nodes must be compiled (they're C++ by definition) -->

## What's Next

- **Next →** [The Sampling Engine](/v2/architecture/sampling-engine) — sample maps, disk streaming, and HLAC compression
- **Build one →** [Building DSP Networks](/v2/guide/dsp-networks) — hands-on guide to building and compiling a scriptnode network
- **Build one →** [Building an Effect](/v2/guide/building-an-effect) — apply scriptnode to an effect plugin

text: Modulator types in depth, chain mechanics, global modulators, and the Modulation Matrix
body:
[Signal Flow](/v2/architecture/audio-signal-path) introduced the basics: every generator has `GainModulation` and `PitchModulation` chains, three modulator types exist, and modulators stack by multiplication (gain) or addition (pitch). This page goes deeper — the individual modulators, intensity scaling, global modulation sources, and the user-configurable Modulation Matrix. These concepts are particularly important for synthesizer architectures where modulation routing defines the instrument's character.

For hands-on synth building, see [Building a Synth](/v2/guide/building-a-synth).

<!-- TODO: Phase 2 content -->
<!-- This is a SPECIAL page — multiple sections of ~1000w each -->
<!-- Focus: Synth archetype (modulation routing is the heart of synthesis) -->

## The Three Modulator Types in Depth

<!-- TODO: (~1000w) -->
<!--   - VoiceStartModulators — fire once when voice starts, produce a single value -->
<!--     - Velocity: maps MIDI velocity (0–127) to a 0.0–1.0 value via a curve -->
<!--     - Random: random value per voice (humanization) -->
<!--     - KeyNumber: maps note number to a value via a table (keyboard tracking) -->
<!--     - Use for: initial amplitude, initial filter cutoff, pitch offset per note -->
<!--   - TimeVariantModulators — run continuously, produce changing values -->
<!--     - LFO: oscillating waveform (sine, triangle, saw, square, random) with rate and depth -->
<!--     - MidiController: maps a CC number to a continuous value -->
<!--     - PitchWheel: maps pitch wheel position -->
<!--     - Use for: vibrato, expression, tremolo, continuous parameter movement -->
<!--   - EnvelopeModulators — run per voice with time-based shape -->
<!--     - AhdsrEnvelope: Attack, Hold, Decay, Sustain, Release — the workhorse -->
<!--     - SimpleEnvelope: simplified attack/release only -->
<!--     - Use for: amplitude contour, filter sweep over note lifetime -->
<!--   - TABLE: all modulators with type, parameters, and typical chain placement -->

## Chain Mechanics & Intensity

<!-- TODO: (~800w) -->
<!--   - GainModulation: all modulators multiply → final gain multiplier (0.0–1.0) -->
<!--   - PitchModulation: all modulators add → final pitch offset (semitones) -->
<!--   - FXModulation: exists on some effects — modulates effect parameters -->
<!--   - Intensity: per-modulator scaling factor -->
<!--     - For gain: intensity scales the modulator's range (0.5 intensity = half effect) -->
<!--     - For pitch: intensity scales the pitch range in semitones -->
<!--   - Bipolar vs unipolar: gain modulators are unipolar (0–1), pitch can be bipolar (±range) -->
<!--   - The order of modulators in a chain doesn't matter for the math -->
<!--     - (multiplication is commutative, addition is commutative) -->
<!--   - But it affects readability: convention is VoiceStart first, then Envelope, then TimeVariant -->

## GlobalModulatorContainer

<!-- TODO: (~800w) -->
<!--   - Problem: a modulator inside one generator only affects that generator -->
<!--   - Solution: GlobalModulatorContainer — a special container at the root level -->
<!--   - Place modulation sources (LFOs, envelopes) in the GlobalModulatorContainer -->
<!--   - Any generator in the tree can reference them via GlobalModulator proxy -->
<!--   - The proxy appears in the target generator's modulation chain -->
<!--   - Use for: one LFO modulating multiple oscillators, shared envelope across generators -->
<!--   - The GlobalModulatorContainer is placed as a child of the root SynthChain -->
<!--   - Critical for synths with complex modulation routing -->
<!--   - Macro controls: global modulators mapped to UI controls for user-facing mod depth -->

## The Modulation Matrix

<!-- TODO: (~800w) -->
<!--   - Engine.createModulationMatrix() — built-in user-configurable routing -->
<!--   - Sources: any modulator in the GlobalModulatorContainer -->
<!--   - Targets: any parameter with a matrixTargetId property set -->
<!--   - The user drags sources to targets in a FloatingTile UI -->
<!--   - Per-connection depth control (how much the source affects the target) -->
<!--   - The matrixTargetId property: set on components to make them matrix targets -->
<!--   - Use for: synths where end users should configure their own modulation routing -->
<!--   - Not every project needs this — simple instruments use fixed modulation -->
<!--   - Example: a wavetable synth with 3 LFOs, 2 envelopes, and 20 possible targets -->

## What's Next

- **Next →** [The Scripting Model](/v2/architecture/scripting-model) — how scripts wire the module tree, UI, and audio together
- **Build one →** [Building a Synth](/v2/guide/building-a-synth) — apply modulation routing to a real synthesizer project

body:
The [module tree](/v2/architecture/module-tree) supports several sound generator types, but the **sampling engine** is the one most HISE projects are built around. Sample libraries, orchestral instruments, pianos, drum kits — anything that plays back recorded audio relies on HISE's `StreamingSampler` and its supporting systems: sample maps for zone mapping, disk streaming for memory efficiency, HLAC compression for distribution, and multi-mic support for positional audio.

This page covers the concepts. For hands-on sampler building, see [Building a Sampler](/v2/guide/building-a-sampler).

<!-- TODO: (~1000w) -->

<!--   - The solution: preload buffers + background disk streaming -->
<!--   - Preload buffer: configurable size (8192–16384 samples typical) -->
<!--   - On note-on: playback starts immediately from the preload buffer -->
<!--   - Background thread loads the rest from disk as playback continues -->
<!--   - The preload/stream boundary is invisible to the user -->
<!--   - PreloadSize parameter on the sampler controls buffer size -->
<!--   - Trade-off: larger buffer = more RAM but safer streaming; smaller = less RAM but riskier -->
<!--   - Voice count affects streaming load: each voice is an independent stream -->

metadata.title: The Scripting Model
metadata.description: HiseScript, the interface script pattern, module and UI references, and how scripts control your instrument

text:
HiseScript is the control layer of HISE. It doesn't produce audio — the [module tree](/v2/architecture/module-tree) and [signal flow](/v2/architecture/audio-signal-path) handle that. Instead, scripts build the [UI](/v2/architecture/ui-model), process MIDI events, connect knobs to parameters, manage [presets](/v2/architecture/data-model), and orchestrate everything the module tree can't express declaratively.

HiseScript looks like JavaScript — curly braces, familiar operators, `function` keyword — but it's a purpose-built language with stricter variable semantics, no closures, no prototype chain, and a compilation model that JavaScript developers won't expect.

HiseScript looks like JavaScript — curly braces, familiar operators, `function` keyword — but it's a purpose-built language with stricter variable semantics, no closures, no prototype chain, and a compilation model that JavaScript developers won't expect.

metadata.title: The Interface Script Pattern
metadata.description: Every HiseScript project follows the same structural pattern in its main `Interface.js`.

text:
Compilation, Not Interpretation

HiseScript doesn't run continuously. It **compiles**. When you press F5 (or HISE starts up), the engine compiles the code, executes `onInit` once, and waits. After that, only **callbacks** fire — in response to MIDI events, UI interactions, or timers.

![Callback flow from compilation through runtime](/images/v2/architecture/scripting-model-callback-flow.svg)

This means **`onInit` is where you build everything.** Module references, UI components, include files, variable declarations — all of it runs at compile time. By the time a MIDI note arrives or a knob turns, the script's structure is already in place. There is no "startup phase" at runtime; `onInit` *is* the startup phase.

text:
Connecting Script to the Module Tree

This is the bridge between code and audio. Scripts control the module tree through **reference objects** — handles to specific processors obtained once in `onInit`.

| API Call | Returns | Use For |
|----------|---------|---------|
| `Synth.getEffect("name")` | Effect reference | Filter, reverb, EQ, gain control |
| `Synth.getSampler("name")` | Sampler reference | Sample map loading, purge control |
| `Synth.getModulator("name")` | Modulator reference | LFO rate, envelope shape |
| `Synth.getMidiProcessor("name")` | MIDI processor reference | Bypass, attribute control |
| `Synth.getChildSynth("name")` | Sound generator reference | Bypass, voice control |

The string argument matches the **ID** in the Module Tree Editor — the name shown on each processor and in the XML preset.

### setAttribute: How Script Becomes Sound

Once you have a reference, `setAttribute` changes any parameter:

```javascript
const var filter = Synth.getEffect("PolyphonicFilter");
const var reverb = Synth.getEffect("SimpleReverb");
const var vibrato = Synth.getModulator("VibratoLFO");

// Each module type exposes named parameter constants
filter.setAttribute(filter.Frequency, 2000);
filter.setAttribute(filter.Q, 0.7);
reverb.setAttribute(reverb.Mix, 0.35);
vibrato.setAttribute(vibrato.Frequency, 4.5);
```

The parameter constants (`filter.Frequency`, `reverb.Mix`) are auto-generated from the module type. The change takes effect on the next audio buffer.

**This is the core mechanism:** knob turns → callback fires → `setAttribute` updates a module parameter → the audio engine hears the change.

You can also read back and bypass:

```javascript
local freq = filter.getAttribute(filter.Frequency);
filter.setBypassed(true);   // remove from signal chain
filter.setBypassed(false);  // re-enable
```

Bypassing removes a processor from the signal chain without deleting it. This is how `MidiMuter` switching works — toggling bypass on parallel samplers to switch articulations instantly.

text:
Variable Types & Thread Safety

HiseScript has four variable types. The choice determines thread safety and lifetime:

| Type | Lifetime | Thread Safety | Use For |
|------|----------|---------------|---------|
| `const var` | Script lifetime | Safe everywhere | Module references, UI handles, lookup tables |
| `var` | Script lifetime | Scripting thread only | UI state: page index, mode flags |
| `reg` | Script lifetime | Audio-thread safe | MIDI callback state: RR counters, last note |
| `local` | Function scope | Always safe | Loop variables, temporary calculations |

```javascript
const var filter = Synth.getEffect("Filter");   // immutable reference
var currentPage = 0;                             // UI state
reg lastNote = -1;                               // MIDI state (audio thread)

inline function doSomething() {
    local i = 0;                                 // temporary
};
```

**The rule:** `const var` for shared references. `reg` for state that MIDI callbacks touch on the audio thread. `var` for scripting-thread-only state. `local` for temporaries. `inline function` for all reusable logic — helpers, callbacks, utilities.

**Threading note:** MIDI callbacks run on the audio thread by default. `Synth.deferCallbacks(true)` moves them to the scripting thread — losing sample-accurate timing but enabling heavy operations like sample map loading. Most sampler projects defer; synths with tight timing requirements may not.

text: What is HISE and who is it for
body:
HISE is an open-source framework for building virtual instruments and audio plugins. You design an audio architecture in a visual processor graph called the **module tree**, write logic in **HiseScript** (a JavaScript-like scripting language), build a custom UI, and export a finished product as a VST3, AU, AAX, or Standalone application — all from a single IDE.

## What You Can Build

Every HISE project falls into one of three archetypes. Each uses the same core tools but emphasizes different parts of the engine.

### Sampler — Sample-Based Instruments

Pianos, orchestral libraries, drum kits, sound design tools. You map recorded audio across the keyboard, add velocity layers and round-robin variations, and build a playback engine around it.

Here's the module tree of a typical sampler project — a hierarchical view of its audio architecture. Each line is a processor: sound generators that produce audio, modulators that shape it, effects that process it, and MIDI processors that handle input.

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── MidiProcessorChain
│   ├── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
│   └── ScriptProcessor "Articulation Handler"
├── StreamingSampler "Sustain"
│   ├── GainModulation
│   │   ├── AHDSR "Volume Envelope"
│   │   └── Velocity Modulator
│   └── EffectChain
│       └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"
├── StreamingSampler "Staccato"
│   └── GainModulation
│       └── AHDSR "Volume Envelope"
└── EffectChain
    └── SimpleReverb "Room"
```

Multiple samplers run in parallel for different articulations. MIDI processors handle keyswitch logic. Effects shape the final output. This pattern scales from a five-sample demo to libraries with multi-mic positions, hundreds of velocity layers, and thousands of mapped zones.

### Synthesizer — Oscillators & Synthesis

Subtractive synths, wavetable instruments, FM engines. You combine sound generators with filters, envelopes, and modulation to create sounds from scratch.

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
├── SynthGroup "Oscillators"
│   └── WavetableSynth "OSC 1"
│       ├── GainModulation
│       │   ├── AHDSR "Amp Envelope"
│       │   └── Velocity Modulator
│       ├── PitchModulation
│       │   └── LFO "Vibrato"
│       └── EffectChain
│           └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"
└── EffectChain
    ├── Delay "Stereo Delay"
    └── SimpleReverb "Reverb"
```

Synth projects range from a single oscillator with a filter to multi-oscillator engines with modulation matrices, scriptnode-based DSP, and hundreds of presets.

### Effect — Audio Processing Plugins

Reverbs, compressors, EQ suites, multi-effect chains. No sound generators — the plugin processes incoming audio from your DAW.

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
└── EffectChain
    ├── Convolution "IR Reverb"
    ├── CurveEQ "Parametric EQ"
    └── SimpleGain "Output"
```

Effect plugins are the leanest archetype. A convolution reverb ships as a complete product with 64 lines of HiseScript and 5 UI controls. Multi-effect suites with mid/side processing and advanced routing use the same structure — more processors in the chain, same pattern.

## The Complexity Spectrum

HISE scales from weekend projects to commercial products. These numbers come from real, shipping plugins:

| | Simple Effect | Mid-Size Synth | Large Drum Machine |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Scripts** | 1 file, 64 lines | 10 files, namespaced | 112 files, Data/UI separation |
| **Module tree** | 3 processors | 36 processors | 289 processors (generated) |
| **UI Controls** | 5 knobs | ~50 controls, 4 pages | 500+ controls, channel mixer |
| **Presets** | 0 | 7 | 1,610 |
| **Custom DSP** | None | 25 scriptnode networks | 19 networks + custom C++ nodes |

The framework handles all of this. You start with the structure your project needs and layer on complexity as it demands.

## How HISE Works

HISE gives you four layers. Every project uses some combination of these:

<!-- GRAPHIC: Diagram of the 4 HISE layers as stacked blocks — Module Tree at the base, Scripting and UI side by side above it, Scriptnode as an optional overlay. Arrows showing how they interact. -->

- **Module tree** — Your audio architecture. You build it visually in the IDE by adding and connecting processors: sound generators, effects, modulators, and MIDI processors. This is the skeleton of your plugin.
- **HiseScript** — The scripting layer. You write logic for MIDI processing, parameter connections, and state management. Scripts run on a dedicated thread, separate from the audio engine.
- **Scriptnode** — The node-based DSP system. When you need custom audio processing beyond the built-in modules, you build DSP networks from nodes — or write your own in Faust or C++.
- **UI system** — Your plugin's interface. You place controls visually in the Interface Designer, connect them to module parameters, and style everything with Look and Feel objects or CSS.

You don't need all four from day one. The [Hello World](/v2/getting-started/hello-world) tutorial uses only the module tree. [Your First Plugin](/v2/getting-started/first-plugin) adds a UI and parameter connections. Scripting and scriptnode come in when your project needs them.

## How This Documentation Is Organized

The docs follow a progressive learning path:

::CardGroup
  ::Card{title="Getting Started" to="/v2/getting-started/installation"}
  You are here. Install HISE, learn the IDE, build your first sound, export a plugin. Linear path — read in order.
  ::
  ::Card{title="Architecture" to="/v2/architecture/overview"}
  Understand *why* HISE works the way it does: the module tree, signal flow, scripting model, and the systems behind every project.
  ::
  ::Card{title="Guide" to="/v2/guide/building-a-sampler"}
  Build real things. Tutorials for samplers, synths, and effects. Practicals for architecture decisions and advanced topics. How-tos for exporting, expansions, and tools.
  ::
  ::Card{title="Reference & API" to="/v2/reference/audio-modules"}
  Look things up. Every module, every scriptnode node, every UI component, every API method.
  ::
::

Start here, follow the path, and branch out when you need to.

## What's Next

- **Get set up →** [Installation](/v2/getting-started/installation)

### Synthesizer — Oscillators & Synthesis

Subtractive synths, wavetable instruments, FM engines. You combine sound generators with filters, envelopes, and modulation to create sounds from scratch.

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
├── SynthGroup "Oscillators"
│   └── WavetableSynth "OSC 1"
│       ├── GainModulation
│       │   ├── AHDSR "Amp Envelope"
│       │   └── Velocity Modulator
│       ├── PitchModulation
│       │   └── LFO "Vibrato"
│       └── EffectChain
│           └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"
└── EffectChain
    ├── Delay "Stereo Delay"
    └── SimpleReverb "Reverb"
```

Synth projects range from a single oscillator with a filter to multi-oscillator engines with modulation matrices, scriptnode-based DSP, and hundreds of presets.

### Effect — Audio Processing Plugins

Reverbs, compressors, EQ suites, multi-effect chains. No sound generators — the plugin processes incoming audio from your DAW.

```
SynthChain "Master Chain"
├── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
└── EffectChain
    ├── Convolution "IR Reverb"
    ├── CurveEQ "Parametric EQ"
    └── SimpleGain "Output"
```

Effect plugins are the leanest archetype. A convolution reverb ships as a complete product with 64 lines of HiseScript and 5 UI controls. Multi-effect suites with mid/side processing and advanced routing use the same structure — more processors in the chain, same pattern.

Every HISE project falls into one of three archetypes. Each uses the same core tools but emphasizes different parts of the engine.

│   │   └── Velocity Modulator
│   └── EffectChain
│       └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"
├── StreamingSampler "Staccato"
│   └── GainModulation

└── EffectChain
    └── SimpleReverb "Room"

text:
The Complexity Spectrum

HISE scales from weekend projects to commercial products. These numbers come from real, shipping plugins:

| | Simple Effect | Mid-Size Synth | Large Drum Machine |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Scripts** | 1 file, 64 lines | 10 files, namespaced | 112 files, Data/UI separation |
| **Module tree** | 3 processors | 36 processors | 289 processors (generated) |
| **UI Controls** | 5 knobs | ~50 controls, 4 pages | 500+ controls, channel mixer |
| **Presets** | 0 | 7 | 1,610 |
| **Custom DSP** | None | 25 scriptnode networks | 19 networks + custom C++ nodes |

The framework handles all of this. You start with the structure your project needs and layer on complexity as it demands.

text:
How HISE Works

HISE gives you four layers. Every project uses some combination of these:

<!-- GRAPHIC: Diagram of the 4 HISE layers as stacked blocks — Module Tree at the base, Scripting and UI side by side above it, Scriptnode as an optional overlay. Arrows showing how they interact. -->

- **Module tree** — Your audio architecture. You build it visually in the IDE by adding and connecting processors: sound generators, effects, modulators, and MIDI processors. This is the skeleton of your plugin.
- **HiseScript** — The scripting layer. You write logic for MIDI processing, parameter connections, and state management. Scripts run on a dedicated thread, separate from the audio engine.
- **Scriptnode** — The node-based DSP system. When you need custom audio processing beyond the built-in modules, you build DSP networks from nodes — or write your own in Faust or C++.
- **UI system** — Your plugin's interface. You place controls visually in the Interface Designer, connect them to module parameters, and style everything with Look and Feel objects or CSS.

You don't need all four from day one. The [Hello World](/v2/getting-started/hello-world) tutorial uses only the module tree. [Your First Plugin](/v2/getting-started/first-plugin) adds a UI and parameter connections. Scripting and scriptnode come in when your project needs them.

text: Step-by-step guide to building a sample-based instrument plugin
body:
By the end of this guide, you'll have a working sample-based instrument with velocity layers, an AHDSR envelope, a filter, a connected UI, and keyswitch-based articulation switching — the same architecture used by shipping HISE products

::Prerequisites
---
items:
  - label: "The Module Tree"
    to: "/v2/architecture/module-tree"
  - label: "The Sampling Engine"
    to: "/v2/architecture/sampling-engine"
  - label: "The UI Model"
    to: "/v2/architecture/ui-model"
  - label: "Parameter Connections"
    to: "/v2/architecture/data-flow-messaging"
---
::

## What We're Building

<!-- GRAPHIC: UI mockup of the finished sampler — 5 knobs (Volume, Attack, Release, Filter Freq, Filter Q), an articulation selector dropdown, and a keyboard at the bottom. Clean, minimal layout. -->

The target architecture at the end of this guide:

```
SynthChain "My Sampler"
├── MidiProcessorChain
│   ├── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
│   └── ScriptProcessor "Articulation Handler"
├── StreamingSampler "Sustain"
│   ├── GainModulation
│   │   ├── AhdsrEnvelope "VolumeEnv"
│   │   └── Velocity "VelMod"
│   └── EffectChain
│       └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"
├── StreamingSampler "Staccato"
│   ├── GainModulation
│   │   └── AhdsrEnvelope "VolumeEnv"
│   └── EffectChain
│       └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"
└── EffectChain
    └── SimpleReverb "Reverb"
```

We'll build this progressively. Each part adds a layer of functionality — you can stop at any point and have something that works.

## Part 1: A Single Sampler

Create a new HISE project (`File → New Project`). In the Module Tree Editor, build this structure:

1. Right-click the `SynthChain` → **Add Sound Generator** → `StreamingSampler`. Name it `Sustain`.
2. Right-click the `SynthChain`'s `MidiProcessorChain` → **Add MIDI Processor** → `ScriptProcessor`. Name it `Interface`.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: Module Tree Editor after Step 2 — SynthChain with a ScriptProcessor "Interface" and a StreamingSampler "Sustain" -->

Your tree looks like this:

```
SynthChain "My Sampler"
├── MidiProcessorChain
│   └── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
└── StreamingSampler "Sustain"
```

Now open the `Interface` ScriptProcessor and add the frontend initialization:

```javascript
Content.makeFrontInterface(600, 400);
Synth.deferCallbacks(true);
```

`Synth.deferCallbacks(true)` moves MIDI callbacks off the audio thread — this is **required** for any sampler project. Without it, operations like loading sample maps or accessing UI state from `onNoteOn` would cause audio glitches. Every sampler project in the HISE ecosystem uses this. See [Signal Flow & Threading](/v2/architecture/audio-signal-path) for the full explanation.

### Import Samples and Create a SampleMap

Open the `Sustain` sampler by double-clicking it. The **Sample Map Editor** opens.

1. Drag your audio files into the Sample Map Editor. HISE maps them automatically based on filename conventions, or you can set the root note, key range, and velocity range manually.
2. Arrange samples across the keyboard. For now, even a single sample mapped to a range works — we'll add velocity layers next.
3. Save the SampleMap: **File → Save SampleMap** → name it `Sustain`.

<!-- ANNOTATED_SCREENSHOT: Sample Map Editor — samples mapped across the keyboard. Labels pointing to root note, key range (LoKey/HiKey), velocity range (LoVel/HiVel). -->

::Tip{title="No samples handy?"}
You can use any WAV or AIFF files. Record a few notes from a software synth, grab free samples from the internet, or use HISE's built-in test tone by adding a `WaveSynth` temporarily.
::

Play some MIDI notes. You should hear your samples.

<!-- HISE_SNIPPET: State after Part 1 — SynthChain with Interface ScriptProcessor and StreamingSampler "Sustain" with a basic SampleMap loaded -->

## Part 2: Velocity Layers and Round-Robin

A single sample per key sounds static. Velocity layers add dynamic expression; round-robin groups add variation.

### Velocity Layers

In the Sample Map Editor, import multiple samples per key at different dynamic levels. Set each sample's velocity range:

- Soft sample: `LoVel = 0`, `HiVel = 42`
- Medium sample: `LoVel = 43`, `HiVel = 84`
- Hard sample: `LoVel = 85`, `HiVel = 127`

The sampler automatically selects the right layer based on how hard you play.

### Round-Robin Groups

For samples with the same note and velocity range, assign different **RR Groups**. The sampler cycles through them on repeated notes, avoiding the "machine gun" effect.

In the Sample Map Editor, select a sample and set its `RRGroup` property (1, 2, 3...). Samples with the same mapping but different RR groups cycle automatically.

<!-- ANNOTATED_SCREENSHOT: Sample Map Editor showing 3 velocity layers × 2 RR groups for a single key. Highlight the LoVel/HiVel and RRGroup properties. -->

## Part 3: Envelope and Filter

### Add an AHDSR Envelope

Right-click the `Sustain` sampler's **GainModulation** chain → **Add Modulator** → `AhdsrEnvelope`. Name it `VolumeEnv`.

This shapes the amplitude of every note: attack fades in, sustain holds, release fades out. Without it, notes cut off abruptly when you release a key.

### Add a Velocity Modulator

In the same **GainModulation** chain, add a `Velocity` modulator. This scales note volume based on how hard you play — complementing the velocity layers with continuous dynamic response.

### Add a Polyphonic Filter

Right-click the `Sustain` sampler's **EffectChain** → **Add Effect** → `PolyphonicFilter`. Name it `Filter`.

This filter runs **per-voice** — each note gets its own independent filter instance. Place it inside the sampler, not on the master chain. See [Architecture Overview](/v2/architecture/overview) for why this matters.

Your tree now:

```
SynthChain "My Sampler"
├── MidiProcessorChain
│   └── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
└── StreamingSampler "Sustain"
    ├── GainModulation
    │   ├── AhdsrEnvelope "VolumeEnv"
    │   └── Velocity "VelMod"
    └── EffectChain
        └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"
```

Play notes — you should hear a shaped, filtered sound with velocity dynamics.

<!-- HISE_SNIPPET: State after Part 3 — StreamingSampler with AHDSR, Velocity modulator, and PolyphonicFilter -->

## Part 4: Build the UI

Open the `Interface` ScriptProcessor and switch to the **Interface Designer**. Set the canvas to 600×400.

### Add Controls

Add these components via the Interface Designer toolbar:

- **ScriptSlider** `knobVolume` — master volume
- **ScriptSlider** `knobAttack` — envelope attack time
- **ScriptSlider** `knobRelease` — envelope release time
- **ScriptSlider** `knobFilterFreq` — filter cutoff frequency
- **ScriptSlider** `knobFilterQ` — filter resonance

<!-- SCREENSHOT: Interface Designer showing the 5 knobs laid out in a row -->

### Connect Parameters

The fastest way to connect a knob to a module parameter is the **zero-code** approach: set `processorId` and `parameterId` on each component. The Connection Wizard in the Interface Designer automates this — right-click a knob, select **Connect to Module Parameter**, and pick the target.

For the knobs that map 1:1 to a module parameter:

| Knob | `processorId` | `parameterId` |
|------|--------------|--------------|
| `knobAttack` | `VolumeEnv` | `Attack` |
| `knobRelease` | `VolumeEnv` | `Release` |
| `knobFilterFreq` | `Filter` | `Frequency` |
| `knobFilterQ` | `Filter` | `Q` |

For the volume knob, we want to control the master chain's output, so we'll use a scripted callback that gives us more control:

```javascript
const var masterGain = Synth.getEffect("Sustain"); // ← the sampler itself has a gain parameter

inline function onKnobVolumeControl(component, value)
{
    Synth.setAttribute(Synth.Volume, value);
};
Content.getComponent("knobVolume").setControlCallback(onKnobVolumeControl);
```

::Tip{title="processorId vs setControlCallback"}
Use `processorId`/`parameterId` when a knob maps directly to one parameter with no logic. Switch to `setControlCallback` when you need arithmetic, multiple targets, or conditional behavior. See [Parameter Connections](/v2/architecture/data-flow-messaging) for the full escalation path.
::

Move the knobs, hear the changes. The filter cutoff should sweep audibly; attack and release should shape the note contour.

<!-- HISE_SNIPPET: State after Part 4 — Sampler with UI connected. 5 knobs wired to parameters. -->

## Part 5: Articulation Switching

A single sampler handles one articulation. Real instruments need multiple — sustain, staccato, pizzicato. HISE handles this with **parallel samplers and a MIDI muter**, not by swapping sample maps at runtime.

### Add a Second Sampler

1. Add another `StreamingSampler` to the `SynthChain`. Name it `Staccato`.
2. Give it the same internal structure: `AhdsrEnvelope` on GainModulation, `PolyphonicFilter` on EffectChain.
3. Import your staccato samples and create a SampleMap named `Staccato`.

### Add a Master Reverb

While we're here, add a `SimpleReverb` to the `SynthChain`'s master EffectChain. Both articulations share this reverb — it runs once on the summed output.

### Set Up the MIDI Muter

1. Add a second `ScriptProcessor` to the `MidiProcessorChain`. Name it `Articulation Handler`.

This script listens for keyswitches (low notes outside the playable range) and mutes/unmutes the appropriate sampler. 

```javascript
// Articulation Handler script
Synth.deferCallbacks(true);

// References to both samplers' MIDI muters
const var muters = [Synth.getMidiProcessor("Sustain"),
                    Synth.getMidiProcessor("Staccato")];

// Keyswitch range — C0 and C#0 (MIDI notes 24-25)
const var KEYSWITCH_LOW = 24;
const var KEYSWITCH_HIGH = 25;

reg currentArticulation = 0;

function onNoteOn()
{
    local n = Message.getNoteNumber();
    
    if (n >= KEYSWITCH_LOW && n <= KEYSWITCH_HIGH)
    {
        Message.ignoreEvent(true);
        currentArticulation = n - KEYSWITCH_LOW;
        
        for (i = 0; i < muters.length; i++)
            muters[i].setAttribute(0, i == currentArticulation ? 0 : 1);
    }
}

function onNoteOff() {}
function onController() {}
function onTimer() {}
```

The key points:
- `Message.ignoreEvent(true)` prevents the keyswitch note from triggering a sample
- Attribute `0` on a `MidiMuter` is the bypass toggle — `0` means active (passing MIDI through), `1` means muted
- `reg currentArticulation` uses a `reg` variable because it's written in a MIDI callback — `var` would work here too since we deferred callbacks, but `reg` is the conventional choice for mutable state accessed in callbacks

### Add a UI Selector

Back in the `Interface` script, add a `ScriptComboBox` for articulation selection:

```javascript
const var cmbArticulation = Content.getComponent("cmbArticulation");
cmbArticulation.set("items", "Sustain\nStaccato");

// Reference the Articulation Handler's muters
const var articulationMuters = [Synth.getMidiProcessor("Sustain"),
                                Synth.getMidiProcessor("Staccato")];

inline function onCmbArticulationControl(component, value)
{
    local idx = value - 1; // ComboBox values are 1-based
    for (i = 0; i < articulationMuters.length; i++)
        articulationMuters[i].setAttribute(0, i == idx ? 0 : 1);
};
cmbArticulation.setControlCallback(onCmbArticulationControl);
```

Now you can switch articulations via the UI dropdown or via MIDI keyswitches. Both paths converge on the same muters.

Your completed module tree:

```
SynthChain "My Sampler"
├── MidiProcessorChain
│   ├── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
│   └── ScriptProcessor "Articulation Handler"
├── StreamingSampler "Sustain"
│   ├── GainModulation
│   │   ├── AhdsrEnvelope "VolumeEnv"
│   │   └── Velocity "VelMod"
│   └── EffectChain
│       └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"
├── StreamingSampler "Staccato"
│   ├── GainModulation
│   │   └── AhdsrEnvelope "VolumeEnv"
│   └── EffectChain
│       └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"
└── EffectChain
    └── SimpleReverb "Reverb"
```

Play notes, switch articulations with keyswitches or the dropdown. Both samplers respond independently with their own envelopes and filters, and share the master reverb.

<!-- HISE_SNIPPET: Completed state — multi-articulation sampler with UI, envelope, filter, keyswitch switching, and master reverb -->

## Part 6: Going Further

This sampler covers the core patterns. From here, production projects add:

- **Multi-mic routing** — add `SimpleGain` effects per mic position inside each sampler, controlled by mic level knobs. See [Sampler Patterns](/v2/examples/sampler-patterns) for the pattern.
- **Velocity crossfades** — set `LowerVelocityXFade` and `UpperVelocityXFade` in the SampleMap for smooth transitions between layers instead of hard switches.
- **Factory presets** — create `.preset` files in `UserPresets/` with category subfolders. Add a `PresetBrowser` FloatingTile to the UI. See [The Preset System](/v2/guide/preset-system).
- **HLAC compression** — convert your samples to monolith `.ch1` files for shipping. This is lossless compression at 45–70% size reduction.
- **Custom UI** — style your knobs with Look and Feel objects or CSS. See [Custom UI Design](/v2/guide/custom-ui).

text:
Part 1: A Single Sampler

Create a new HISE project (`File → New Project`). In the Module Tree Editor, build this structure:

1. Right-click the `SynthChain` → **Add Sound Generator** → `StreamingSampler`. Name it `Sustain`.
2. Right-click the `SynthChain`'s `MidiProcessorChain` → **Add MIDI Processor** → `ScriptProcessor`. Name it `Interface`.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: Module Tree Editor after Step 2 — SynthChain with a ScriptProcessor "Interface" and a StreamingSampler "Sustain" -->

Your tree looks like this:

```
SynthChain "My Sampler"
├── MidiProcessorChain
│   └── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
└── StreamingSampler "Sustain"
```

Now open the `Interface` ScriptProcessor and add the frontend initialization:

```javascript
Content.makeFrontInterface(600, 400);
Synth.deferCallbacks(true);
```

`Synth.deferCallbacks(true)` moves MIDI callbacks off the audio thread — this is **required** for any sampler project. Without it, operations like loading sample maps or accessing UI state from `onNoteOn` would cause audio glitches. Every sampler project in the HISE ecosystem uses this. See [Signal Flow & Threading](/v2/architecture/audio-signal-path) for the full explanation.

### Import Samples and Create a SampleMap

Open the `Sustain` sampler by double-clicking it. The **Sample Map Editor** opens.

1. Drag your audio files into the Sample Map Editor. HISE maps them automatically based on filename conventions, or you can set the root note, key range, and velocity range manually.
2. Arrange samples across the keyboard. For now, even a single sample mapped to a range works — we'll add velocity layers next.
3. Save the SampleMap: **File → Save SampleMap** → name it `Sustain`.

<!-- ANNOTATED_SCREENSHOT: Sample Map Editor — samples mapped across the keyboard. Labels pointing to root note, key range (LoKey/HiKey), velocity range (LoVel/HiVel). -->



Play some MIDI notes. You should hear your samples.

text:
Part 2: Velocity Layers and Round-Robin

A single sample per key sounds static. Velocity layers add dynamic expression; round-robin groups add variation.

### Velocity Layers

In the Sample Map Editor, import multiple samples per key at different dynamic levels. Set each sample's velocity range:

- Soft sample: `LoVel = 0`, `HiVel = 42`
- Medium sample: `LoVel = 43`, `HiVel = 84`
- Hard sample: `LoVel = 85`, `HiVel = 127`

The sampler automatically selects the right layer based on how hard you play.

### Round-Robin Groups

For samples with the same note and velocity range, assign different **RR Groups**. The sampler cycles through them on repeated notes, avoiding the "machine gun" effect.

In the Sample Map Editor, select a sample and set its `RRGroup` property (1, 2, 3...). Samples with the same mapping but different RR groups cycle automatically.

<!-- ANNOTATED_SCREENSHOT: Sample Map Editor showing 3 velocity layers × 2 RR groups for a single key. Highlight the LoVel/HiVel and RRGroup properties. -->

text:
Part 3: Envelope and Filter

### Add an AHDSR Envelope

Right-click the `Sustain` sampler's **GainModulation** chain → **Add Modulator** → `AhdsrEnvelope`. Name it `VolumeEnv`.

This shapes the amplitude of every note: attack fades in, sustain holds, release fades out. Without it, notes cut off abruptly when you release a key.

### Add a Velocity Modulator

In the same **GainModulation** chain, add a `Velocity` modulator. This scales note volume based on how hard you play — complementing the velocity layers with continuous dynamic response.

### Add a Polyphonic Filter

Right-click the `Sustain` sampler's **EffectChain** → **Add Effect** → `PolyphonicFilter`. Name it `Filter`.

This filter runs **per-voice** — each note gets its own independent filter instance. Place it inside the sampler, not on the master chain. See [Architecture Overview](/v2/architecture/overview) for why this matters.

Your tree now:

```
SynthChain "My Sampler"
├── MidiProcessorChain
│   └── ScriptProcessor "Interface"
└── StreamingSampler "Sustain"
    ├── GainModulation
    │   ├── AhdsrEnvelope "VolumeEnv"
    │   └── Velocity "VelMod"
    └── EffectChain
        └── PolyphonicFilter "Filter"
```

Play notes — you should hear a shaped, filtered sound with velocity dynamics.

<!-- HISE_SNIPPET: State after Part 3 — StreamingSampler with AHDSR, Velocity modulator, and PolyphonicFilter -->

text:
Part 4: Build the UI

Open the `Interface` ScriptProcessor and switch to the **Interface Designer**. Set the canvas to 600×400.

### Add Controls

Add these components via the Interface Designer toolbar:

- **ScriptSlider** `knobVolume` — master volume
- **ScriptSlider** `knobAttack` — envelope attack time
- **ScriptSlider** `knobRelease` — envelope release time
- **ScriptSlider** `knobFilterFreq` — filter cutoff frequency
- **ScriptSlider** `knobFilterQ` — filter resonance

<!-- SCREENSHOT: Interface Designer showing the 5 knobs laid out in a row -->

### Connect Parameters

The fastest way to connect a knob to a module parameter is the **zero-code** approach: set `processorId` and `parameterId` on each component. The Connection Wizard in the Interface Designer automates this — right-click a knob, select **Connect to Module Parameter**, and pick the target.

For the knobs that map 1:1 to a module parameter:

| Knob | `processorId` | `parameterId` |
|------|--------------|--------------|
| `knobAttack` | `VolumeEnv` | `Attack` |
| `knobRelease` | `VolumeEnv` | `Release` |
| `knobFilterFreq` | `Filter` | `Frequency` |
| `knobFilterQ` | `Filter` | `Q` |

For the volume knob, we want to control the master chain's output, so we'll use a scripted callback that gives us more control:

```javascript
const var masterGain = Synth.getEffect("Sustain"); // ← the sampler itself has a gain parameter

inline function onKnobVolumeControl(component, value)
{
    Synth.setAttribute(Synth.Volume, value);
};
Content.getComponent("knobVolume").setControlCallback(onKnobVolumeControl);
```



Move the knobs, hear the changes. The filter cutoff should sweep audibly; attack and release should shape the note contour.

<!-- HISE_SNIPPET: State after Part 4 — Sampler with UI connected. 5 knobs wired to parameters. -->
